Unlocking asynchronicity in continuous batching

📅 14 May 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: we explain how to separate CPU and GPU workloads to get a massive performance boost for inference.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is the second post in a series on efficient LLM inference.
  • An H200 costs around $5 an hour on Inference Endpoints.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: we explain how to separate CPU and GPU workloads to get a massive performance boost for inference.

Recent findings suggest that this is the second post in a series on efficient LLM inference. The first post covered continuous batching from first principles. It introduces some concepts we build upon: KV cache, FlashAttention, attention masks, etc.

An H200 costs around $5 an hour on Inference Endpoints. That's cheap for an hour, but use it for a day and you are already paying $120. If this is the case, you want your GPU to be used to its fullest.We have seen that Continuous Batching improves GPU utilization by scheduling tightly packed batches, so no compute is wasted on padding. But there is a second source of waste that continuous batching does not address: by default, it is synchronous. This means the CPU and GPU take turns: while the GPU computes, the CPU waits. And while the CPU prepares the next batch, the GPU waits. In a loop running hundreds of steps per second, those idle gaps add up, and as we will show, they can account for nearly a quarter of total runtime. To ensure the GPU is busy computing 100% of the time, we need to get rid of those gaps.

To achieve this, we can use asynchronous batching: we are going to disentangle CPU batch preparation from GPU batch compute, so both can run in parallel and we always have a productive GPU 🔥.

This is how naive synchronous batching works:.

When the CPU prepares a fresh batch, it selects which requests to include, updates the KV cache table, evicts requests that finished in the previous runs, and admits new ones to fill the freed space. Once that is done, it transfers the prepared inputs to the GPU. The GPU runs its forward pass and samples (i.e. chooses) a new token for each request. The results come back to the CPU, so it knows what token each request just produced, then the whole cycle repeats again.

Notice the red annotation on the right: after the GPU finishes computing, it goes idle. The next batch cannot start until the CPU has gone through its revision step: sampling the output tokens, updating request states, re-scheduling the batch.

According to recent reports, this is the core inefficiency of synchronous batching: the CPU and GPU take turns. While the GPU is computing, the CPU is idle. While the CPU is updating, the GPU is idle. In no circumstances are they both doing useful work at the same time. For a single forward pass this might seem like a small price to pay, but in a continuous batching loop running hundreds of steps per second, these idle gaps accumulate into real throughput loss.

To showcase this, we profile the time spent on CPU and GPU when generating 8K tokens with a batch size of 32 using an 8B model:.

If you want to produce the same kind of graph, you can instrument the continuous batching code to dump CPU and GPU activity spans and use this script.

According to recent reports, the timeline alternates between green (GPU active, CPU idle) and red (CPU active, GPU idle): the two never overlap. Total generation time is 300.6 seconds, with 24.0% of that spent with an idle GPU waiting for the CPU to finish. Nearly a quarter of all generation time is wasted, from the point of view of the GPU. This is the pessimistic way of viewing things.

According to recent reports, the optimistic way is that generation time would drop from 300 to 228 seconds (a free 24% speedup!), if we could eliminate CPU overhead entirely. This requires zero upcoming kernel or model changes, just careful coordination of hardware.

It has been revealed that fundamentally, the idea is simple: we need to figure out how to run batch preparation for batch N+1 while batch N is computing. But this simple idea hides a few technical difficulties:.

By answering those questions, we are going to build asynchronous batching from scratch. We followed the same steps to implement it as part of continuous batching in the transformers library. Feel free to check the code and compare!

Our end goal is to have concurrent execution of CPU and GPU operations. We need a way to categorize our operations, so we can let the machine know which operations can run concurrently. We can achieve this using CUDA streams.

In a recent development, to understand how CUDA orders its operations, we need to talk about CUDA streams. A stream is an ordered queue of GPU operations (kernel rolls out, memory copies, synchronization barriers) that executes in the order they were submitted. Every GPU operation is always scheduled inside a stream. Operations within the same stream are sequential: the GPU will not start the next one until the previous has completed. Operations in different streams are independent of each other and can run concurrently. To illustrate, if you launch 3 operations across 3 different streams, execution looks like this:.

In a recent development, all three operations start at the same time. This is a slight simplification: every GPU operation is ultimately initiated by the CPU, and that initiation takes a small amount of time: finding the right kernel, issuing the call, transferring the command from CPU to GPU, etc. This is called CPU launch overhead, and a more realistic diagram looks like this:.

In a recent development, the operations are still concurrent, but their start times are staggered by the cost of each CPU launch. We will keep showing these CPU launch events throughout because they take real time, and they will help us track "what is launched when" as we move to asynchronous workflows. For instance, we will often check if a stream is flushed: that means that all operations in a stream have been executed.

Industry observers note that if you have never explicitly used CUDA streams in PyTorch, you might be surprised they exist at all. A typical PyTorch script never mentions them, and it does not feel like GPU operations are asynchronous: the CPU seems to wait for the GPU to finish before moving on. That feeling is accurate, and it comes from the default stream.

Industry observers note that when you call a PyTorch operation without specifying a stream, it lands on the default stream. The default stream has one special property: it is synchronizing. If an operation is scheduled on the default stream, it waits for all other streams to be flushed, i.e. all work on the GPU has to be over before a single operation on the default stream can start. The reverse is also true: any operation, regardless of its stream, waits for the default stream to be flushed before it debuts.

Sources indicate that so if you transfer to the CPU the result of a default stream operation, even with a transfer that is supposed to be non-blocking for the CPU, your CPU will still block until all GPU operations have finished because the operations were scheduled on the default stream. This effectively destroys any effort to build concurrency.

In a recent development, that's why we need to use non-default streams. Enqueuing a kernel launch or a non-blocking memory copy returns control to the CPU immediately. The GPU will run the operation in the background, but the CPU does not wait. This answers our first question: to get back CPU control after launching GPU work, we use a non-default stream.

For the rest of this post, we will assume all memory transfers from one device to the other are non-blocking. We will therefore have to synchronize them ourselves.

We established that no GPU operation should land on the default stream. But the question remains: if we are not using the default stream, what streams should we use? Let us go back to the synchronous batching figure:.

We can identify three distinct GPU operations:.

Recent findings suggest that this means we need three streams: one for compute, one for CPU-to-GPU transfers, and one for GPU-to-CPU transfers. The transfers are independent, so there is no reason to serialize them, and each one gets its own stream.

In a recent development, A note on nomenclature: when talking about CPUs and GPUs, the convention used throughout the CUDA documentation is to call the CPU the host and the GPU the device. We will use that convention from now on. CPU-to-GPU transfers are called host-to-device (H2D) transfers, and GPU-to-CPU transfers are called device-to-host (D2H) transfers. Hence, the three streams are the H2D stream, the compute stream, and the D2H stream.

Let us now try to use streams to asynchronously launch a batch on the GPU and get back CPU control. From the CPU, we do the following:.

If we do this using only CUDA streams, the results are available almost instantly and they are incorrect. To understand why, let us look at what happened:.

It has been revealed that because streams are independent of each other, all three GPU operations launched at nearly the same time. The compute stream did not wait for the H2D transfer to complete, so the forward pass ran on whatever was already sitting in GPU memory. The D2H stream did not wait for compute to finish, so it transferred results that had not been computed yet. Step 5 returned instantly because nothing was blocking the CPU: there was no default stream to synchronize against.

Recent findings suggest that the operations are all running correctly in isolation. The problem is that we never told the streams to wait for each other. We know that compute must start after H2D completes, and that D2H must start after compute completes, but we did not enforce that ordering. We need a mechanism to say "do not start this operation until that one is done" across stream boundaries.

To enforce synchronization between the streams, we are going to use CUDA events.

A CUDA event is a marker that can be recorded into a stream. When the GPU reaches that marker during execution, it sets the event as completed. Any other stream can then be told to wait for that event before starting its next operation. Concretely, there are two operations: stream.record(event), which inserts the marker into a stream at the current position, and stream.wait(event), which blocks a stream from proceeding until the event is marked complete. Importantly, wait blocks the stream, not the CPU or other streams running in parallel: the CPU call returns immediately, and only the waiting stream is held back.

The figure above highlights a single event synchronizing two streams. The CPU concerns three operations in rapid succession (the three small blocks): launch input preparation on stream 1, record the event on stream 1, then tell stream 2 to wait for it. Then the CPU continues immediately. Stream 1 runs its operation, and when it completes, the event is set. Stream 2 is held at the wait marker the whole time, and only starts compute once the event is marked complete. The CPU was not involved in any of this: the ordering was enforced entirely on the GPU side.

According to recent reports, applied to our case, the fix is straightforward. After enqueueing the H2D transfer, we call h2d_stream.record(h2d_done): the event will be marked as completed only when the transfer finishes. Before enqueueing the forward pass, we call compute_stream.wait(h2d_done), so the compute stream will not start until h2d_done is set. We do the same between compute and D2H: after launching the forward pass with model.forward, we call compute_stream.record(compute_done), then d2h_stream.wait(compute_done) before enqueueing the output transfer. The result is a pipeline with explicit ordering:.

The CPU enqueues all of this in sequence, then moves on. At no point does it block. The GPU enforces the ordering through the events, and all three streams are active as soon as their dependency is satisfied.

Industry observers note that the figure above reveals how this unfolds. The CPU prepares the batch, then rapidly enqueues all the GPU work: the H2D transfer, the forward pass, the D2H transfer, with record and wait calls inserted between each stage. After that, the CPU is free. The GPU takes over, executing each stream in order as its dependency event is set. Notice the green annotation on the right: once the D2H transfer completes, the CPU comes back and reads the results. This final synchronization is the only point where the CPU blocks in the whole step. To implement it, we record a third event on the D2H stream after the output transfer, then call d2h_done_event.synchronize() on the CPU side. synchronize blocks the CPU until the D2H stream reaches that marker.

According to recent reports, this is the key difference from synchronous batching: before, the CPU blocked after every operation. Now, it is free to do "something" while the GPU works.We need to figure out what that "something" is, because right now nothing changed from a GPU-utilization standpoint.

According to recent reports, the window where the CPU is available sits between dispatching batch N and dispatching batch N+1 to the GPU. Its natural use would be to prepare batch N+1's inputs, so we can dispatch them to the GPU and have them be ready once batch N compute is over. Let us see how we can do this.

To prepare batch N+1, we can reuse the same CPU-side objects that prepared batch N: the list of current requests, the state of the cache, the host-side tensor buffers, etc. However, we need to pay attention to two things:.

We address these concerns, data corruption and data transmission, in the next two sections.

In a recent development, first, we are going to tackle the potential data corruption issue.Imagine batch N and batch N+1 share the same device-side input buffers, and that the H2D transfer of batch N+1 inputs starts while batch N is still computing. The CPU may write batch N+1's inputs while the GPU is still reading batch N's from the same memory. So the GPU may pick up partially overwritten data, and the result is corrupted. This is a race condition. The same risk exists on the host side: reusing the same source for the copy while the H2D copy for batch N is still in flight corrupts the transfer.

The fix is to use two sets of tensors and alternate between them. While the GPU processes batch N from slot A, the CPU updates the requests' state with the results of batch N-1. The CPU next prepares batch N+1 in input slot B. Next step, they swap. This is illustrated in the diagram below:.

Of course, this comes with a cost: it doubles the amount of RAM and VRAM used to store the input and output tensors. This is an acceptable tradeoff, especially when using FlashAttention, because it does not require an attention mask, which is by far the largest input tensor.

Recent findings suggest that but having two slots creates another problem. In inference, we usually use CUDA graphs to reduce latency. In a nutshell, a CUDA graph is a pre-recorded sequence of CUDA operations. It is recorded against specific memory addresses: a graph captured for slot A cannot be replayed against slot B's buffers. So we need two graphs. And if each graph has its own memory buffer, that is double the VRAM again.

Industry observers note that the solution is a memory pool: a shared memory buffer that both graphs allocate from. The only constraint is that two graphs in the same pool must never execute concurrently. Since batch N must finish before batch N+1 starts, that is always the case. In practice, both graphs together use nearly the same amount of VRAM as one. We only pay for two captures at initialization time.We can create any number of CUDA graphs in the same pool and the total memory usage is still capped at the maximum across graphs. This is showcased below.

Now that we know how to prevent data corruption, we can address the second glitch: getting the output tokens of batch N into the inputs of batch N+1.

In a recent development, consider a request that appears in both batch N and batch N+1. In batch N, it produces a latest token. That token is its input for batch N+1. The problem is that when we are preparing batch N+1's input buffer, we do not have that token yet: batch N is still running. To address this, we use a placeholder token when building batch N+1. We will use 0 as a placeholder, for reasons that will become apparent later. We replace that placeholder after batch N is done computing and before batch N+1 starts the forward pass. We call that step the carry-over, because we are carrying over the new tokens from batch N to batch N+1. The idea behind carry-over is illustrated below:.

To perform carry-over, we only need three things: the output token ids of batch N, the input token ids of batch N+1, and a tensor with instructions on how to perform carry-over. We will call this tensor the carry-over mask. It contains the target destination for the tokens that need to be carried over, and -1 for the ones that do not. We represent one below:.

The carry-over itself consists of four operations:.

Industry observers note that since those four operations are very cheap, we perform them at the start of each new batch and capture the carry-over in the CUDA graph. If the carry-over mask contains only -1 (a value of -1 means: do not carry over this position) then the last step is an addition with a zero tensor. This does not happen often because decoding requests that span more than one batch are typically scheduled in consecutive batches.

Let us put everything together and trace through the first two steps.

Step 0 is a cold start: there is no previous batch running, so the CPU prepares batch 0 in slot A and dispatches it as it would with synchronous batching. No overlap yet.

Industry observers note that step 1 is where the async loop begins. The GPU is now running batch 0 on slot A, and the CPU is free. It immediately starts preparing batch 1 in slot B: evicting finished requests, admitting new requests, updating the KV cache routing table, building the carry-over mask. All of this runs in full overlap with the GPU. Once batch 1's inputs are ready, the CPU enqueues the work in sequence: it debuts the H2D transfer for slot B, records and waits events for the compute and D2H streams, then moves on.

Sources indicate that now two things happen in parallel on the GPU. On slot A, the GPU finishes compute and sets compute_done, which releases the D2H transfer of batch 0's outputs. On slot B, the H2D transfer of batch 1's inputs is running. Once it completes, the h2d_done event is set and compute for batch 1 begins. The carry-over from batch 0 to batch 1 is part of that compute: it happens before the regular forward pass. Since slot A and slot B are independent, all of this overlaps freely.

The CPU, meanwhile, blocks on d2h_done_event.synchronize() until batch 0's outputs land. Then it processes the outputs, updates the state of all requests that were in batch 0, and starts scheduling batch 2. The loop is now running, and every subsequent step follows exactly the same pattern.We illustrate the full workload below. Each slot has a dedicated color for CPU and GPU operations and for events (which are also slot-specific). For readability's sake, we do not show the CPU's launch of GPU operations (like compute or data movement), but they still take place. This is justified because launching a GPU operation has negligible latency compared to the operations shown.

Sources indicate that as long as batch N+1's inputs are ready on the GPU when batch N finishes, the GPU never idles between batches. The only question is whether the CPU finishes its work before the GPU finishes compute. That is usually the case: models continue to grow while batch scheduling stays relatively cheap, so GPU compute is the bottleneck, not the CPU.

To find out, we run the same experiment as before: 8K tokens, batch size 32, 8B model.

In a recent development, the timeline is almost entirely dark green: CPU and GPU running at the same time. The occasional light green slivers are moments where the GPU is active but the CPU has already finished its prep and is waiting. The near-invisible red marks are the sync points between batches, where the CPU blocks to sample batch N's outputs. The GPU is active for 99.4% of total runtime, up from 76.0%. Total generation time drops from 300.6s to 234.5s, a 22% speedup. We predicted 24% if CPU overhead were fully eliminated. The small remaining gap is that unavoidable sync point. No new kernels, no model changes: letting the CPU and GPU work at the same time.

We started with a synchronous workload where the CPU and GPU worked one after the other, leaving both underused. By moving from schedule-based dependencies to data-based dependencies and refining synchronization points, we managed to disentangle the CPU and GPU workloads, making parallel execution of both hardwares possible. Hence, we were able to saturate the GPU work queue and ensure it is always running. This finally resulted in a large increase of generation speed while maintaining the accuracy of the model. Pretty much a slam dunk.

The full implementation is in the transformers library. If you want to see how this translates to actual code, the general entry point for continuous batching is continuous_batching.py. The more asynchronous-centric code is located in the ContinuousBatchingAsyncIOs class.

Industry observers note that asynchronous batching gets us one step closer to unlocking SOTA throughput for long generation, for generation lengths of 16K+ like in reinforcement learning. But there are still some other, smaller things that are also needed to reach that goal. In the next article, we will go through those: offloading requests, decode-specific kernels or fine-grained compile, among others. Stay tuned!

It has been revealed that wonderful blog! Had a clarification question, on the benefits of a shared memory pool for cuda-graphs. If my understanding is correct the shared memory pool would be memory needed for inputs/outputs of Batch(N) + Batch(N+1). So each cuda graph presumably captures this memory and re-uses it (albeit different slots). Is the benefit of the shared memory pool that it reduces any additional cudagraph overhead?

Also another question, wouldn't it be common for the batch sizes of N and N+1 to be different? If so how is the memory needed for batch N+1 pre-allocated accurately, is it just a max-batch size?

The inputs and outputs are actually pre-allocated static tensors, before any CUDA graph is even created.

Sources indicate that as for why the pool is useful:Say you capture a CUDA graph A: itneeds memory to execute. This memory is needed to store activations or workspace tensors for the kernels debuted in graph A. This allocated memory is owned by graph A.Then, if you create another graph B, it will also allocate some memory for its execution. Because CUDA can't be sure you won't run graph A and B at the same time, the memory allocated for graph A and B can't be the same: you would risk data corruption. But if you can guarantee graph A and B won't run at the same time, then there is no reason not to allocate the same memory to graph A and B. That memory shared between graphs A and B is the memory pool.

It has been revealed that and as a sidenote, if you know which graph is going to need the most memory, you better capture it first. That way, the graph pool has the maximum size right away, and graph you capture afterwards can always fit inside the pool. Whereas if you capture a graph that requires a low amount of memory and then try to capture a graph that requires more memory, you run the risk of having memory fragmentation.

Granite Embedding Multilingual R2: Open Apache 2.0 Multilingual Embeddings with 32K Context — Best Sub-100M Retrieval Quality

📅 14 May 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: Two fresh Apache 2.0 multilingual embedding models built on ModernBERT — a 97M-parameter compact model that beats every open sub-100M multilingual embedder on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval (60.3), and a 311M full-size model that scores 65.2 on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval (#2 among open models under 500M parameters) with Matryoshka support.
  • In this post: Enterprise-Ready by Design · A Strong Sub-100M Multilingual Model · What Changed from R1 · Training the Full-Size 311M Model · Building the compact 97M Multilingual Model · Benchmark Results · Matryoshka Embeddings · Deployment Options · For Framework Integrators · Which Model Should You Use?
  • Recent findings suggest that multilingual embedding models face a persistent tension: broad language coverage usually comes at the cost of model size, and small models usually sacrifice languages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: Two fresh Apache 2.0 multilingual embedding models built on ModernBERT — a 97M-parameter compact model that beats every open sub-100M multilingual embedder on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval (60.3), and a 311M full-size model that scores 65.2 on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval (#2 among open models under 500M parameters) with Matryoshka support. Both cover 200+ languages, are tuned on 52 languages, handle 32K-token context (64x R1), and add code retrieval across 9 programming languages.

In this post: Enterprise-Ready by Design · A Strong Sub-100M Multilingual Model · What Changed from R1 · Training the Full-Size 311M Model · Building the compact 97M Multilingual Model · Benchmark Results · Matryoshka Embeddings · Deployment Options · For Framework Integrators · Which Model Should You Use? · Try The Models.

Recent findings suggest that multilingual embedding models face a persistent tension: broad language coverage usually comes at the cost of model size, and small models usually sacrifice languages. If you work across languages — retrieval-augmented generation over multilingual corpora, cross-lingual search, code retrieval in international teams — you've likely had to choose between a model that's fast enough and one that's good enough.

Recent findings suggest that the Granite Embedding Multilingual R2 release narrows that gap considerably. We're releasing two upcoming multilingual embedding models:.

Recent findings suggest that both models support 200+ languages with enhanced retrieval quality for 52 languages and programming code, handle context lengths up to 32,768 tokens (a 64x increase over their R1 predecessors), and are released under the Apache 2.0 license. They work out of the box with sentence-transformers and transformers, require no task-specific instructions, and are compatible as drop-in replacements in LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and Milvus with a one-line model name change. For frameworks presently using an English-only default, that one line gives every user in your community support for 200+ languages — no API changes, no new dependencies, no code changes required on their end. Both models ship with ONNX and OpenVINO weights for CPU-optimized inference.

Recent findings suggest that the underlying encoder was pretrained on text from 200+ languages, producing general-purpose embeddings for any of them. The following 52 languages receive explicit retrieval-pair and cross-lingual training for higher-quality retrieval:.

Albanian (sq), Arabic (ar), Azerbaijani (az), Bengali (bn), Bulgarian (bg), Catalan (ca), Chinese (zh), Croatian (hr), Czech (cs), Danish (da), Dutch (nl), English (en), Estonian (et), Finnish (fi), French (fr), Georgian (ka), German (de), Greek (el), Hebrew (he), Hindi (hi), Hungarian (hu), Icelandic (is), Indonesian (id), Italian (it), Japanese (ja), Kazakh (kk), Khmer (km), Korean (ko), Latvian (lv), Lithuanian (lt), Malay (ms), Marathi (mr), Norwegian (no), Persian (fa), Polish (pl), Portuguese (pt), Romanian (ro), Russian (ru), Serbian (sr), Slovak (sk), Slovenian (sl), Spanish (es), Swahili (sw), Swedish (sv), Tagalog (tl), Telugu (te), Thai (th), Turkish (tr), Ukrainian (uk), Urdu (ur), Uzbek (uz), Vietnamese (vi).

Additionally, the models are trained on programming code (Python, Go, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Ruby, SQL, C, C++) and support cross-lingual code retrieval.

In a recent development, both embedding models are trained on a mixture of IBM‑curated datasets, publicly available data, and internally generated or synthetic data. Public web‑derived data used in training is selected and filtered using IBM‑developed quality, deduplication, and governance processes intended to reduce risk in downstream commercial use. We intentionally avoid the use of the MS‑MARCO training dataset and datasets with explicit non‑commercial licensing restrictions. The models are pretrained using GneissWeb, an IBM‑curated dataset derived from publicly available web content and processed using IBM’s data preparation and governance tooling—along with additional IBM‑curated and other publicly available sources. Datasets undergo IBM governance review to assess licensing considerations, ownership signals, and personal data risks. These processes are designed to contribute to responsible use and enterprise deployment.

According to recent reports, the standout of this release is granite-embedding-97m-multilingual-r2. At 97 million parameters, it scores 60.3 on Multilingual MTEB Retrieval across 18 languages — the highest retrieval score we've found for any open multilingual embedding model under 100M parameters. The next-best model in that size class, multilingual-e5-small, scores 50.9 on the same benchmark — a +9.4 point gap on a mature benchmark.

At roughly one-third the size of the 311M full-size model, it retains the majority of its retrieval quality across multilingual, code, and long-document benchmarks — a +12.2 point gain on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval over its direct predecessor, driven by a fresh architecture, better training data, and a novel pruning methodology (more on that below). The full-size granite-embedding-311m-multilingual-r2 scores 65.2 on the same benchmark, a +13.0 point gain over its R1 predecessor.

The Granite Embedding Multilingual R1 models were built on XLM-RoBERTa encoders with a 512-token context window. The R2 generation is a ground-up rebuild:.

ModernBERT is a recent encoder architecture that revisits the original BERT design with techniques from the last five years of transformer research. The shift brings several practical benefits: alternating attention lengths reduce computation on long sequences (improves throughput on long sequences significantly), rotary position embeddings allow the 32K context window without the positional interpolation hacks that plague older architectures, and Flash Attention 2.0 support speeds up encoding on modern GPUs.

According to recent reports, the latest multilingual tokenizers are worth highlighting. Rather than reusing XLM-RoBERTa's 250K-token vocabulary, we adopted existing tokenizers with strong multilingual and code coverage. The 311M model uses the Gemma 3 tokenizer (262K tokens); the 97M model starts from the GPT-OSS tokenizer and prunes it down to a compact 180K-token vocabulary that preserves broad multilingual coverage while reducing the embedding table's parameter footprint. Tokenizer efficiency matters more than people realize — a 32K-token window sounds impressive until your tokenizer burns half of it encoding a single paragraph of Thai.

The 311M model is a 22-layer ModernBERT encoder with a 262K-token multilingual vocabulary, trained through a multi-stage pipeline:.

The result is a model that scores 65.2 on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval and 56.3 on the overall average — a +14.5 point average gain over its R1 predecessor.

The 97M model is trained through a combination of vocabulary selection and knowledge distillation:.

Sources indicate that this approach transfers retrieval-specific knowledge from multiple strong teachers, while reducing the model parameters without sacrificing language coverage. The result is a highly efficient compact model — scoring 60.3 on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval vs. 65.2 for the full-size model, while being approximately 3x smaller.

Performance across the main benchmark suite sorted by model size. Scores are averages across tasks within each benchmark (higher is better):.

Encoding speed matters for production workloads, especially when you're indexing millions of documents or need low-latency query encoding. We measured latency and throughput on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU using 512-token chunks:.

The 97M model encodes over 2,500 documents per second — comparable throughput to multilingual-e5-small — while delivering substantially higher retrieval quality. The 311M model, at ~1,800 docs/sec, performs better than jina-embeddings-v5-text-nano on retrieval quality (65.2 vs. 63.3) at over 5.5x the encoding speed (note: speed numbers are computed with the latest transformer code, which had a speed regression vs the last 4.57 version - for both the Jina and granite models - see our technical report for details). harrier-oss-v1-270m offers the best combination of speed and retrieval score among the competitors listed here.

The 311M model supports Matryoshka Representation Learning, which lets you truncate embeddings from the full 768 dimensions down to 512, 384, 256, or 128 with graceful quality degradation. This is useful when storage, memory, or similarity-computation cost is a concern — a 256-dimensional embedding takes one-third the storage of a 768-dimensional one, and cosine similarity is proportionally cheaper to compute.

Here's how retrieval quality holds up across embedding dimensions:.

The quality loss from dimension reduction is remarkably small. Cutting from 768 to 256 dimensions — a 3x reduction in storage and similarity-computation cost — drops MTEB Multilingual Retrieval by just 0.5 points (65.2 → 64.7) and Code Retrieval by 0.5 points (63.9 → 63.4). Even at 128 dimensions (a 6x reduction), the model still scores 63.7 on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval and 62.3 on Code — retaining over 97% of its full-dimension performance. In practice, this means you can substantially reduce your index size and search latency with minimal impact on result quality. (Note,results in the above picture were evaluated with a context length of 1024 for English and Multilingual Retrieval, and 8192 for Code).

For comparison, the 311M model truncated to 384 dimensions (the same dimensionality as the 97M model's native output) still outperforms the 97M model across all three benchmarks. If you need 384-dimensional embeddings and can afford the 311M model's encoding cost, Matryoshka truncation is the stronger option.

The 97M model does not support Matryoshka — 384 dimensions is already compact.

Average performance on cross-lingual tasks within MTEB Retrieval. Belebele measures cross-lingual passage matching across 122 languages; MLQA measures extractive cross-lingual question answering retrieval across 7 languages.

The 311M R2 model gains +4.3 on Belebele and +4.1 on MLQA over its R1 predecessor, showing improved cross-lingual transfer at the larger scale across both benchmarks.

Industry observers note that the 97M R2 model scores lower on Belebele (52.9 vs 55.1, −2.2) while matching its R1 predecessor on MLQA (60.5). The Belebele gap is a tradeoff inherent in the pruning and vocabulary reduction process — the R2 model's training prioritized the broader 18-language MTEB Multilingual Retrieval set (where it gains +12.2 over R1) and long-document retrieval (+31.3), while the smaller vocabulary (180K vs. 250K tokens) and reduced layer count (12 vs. 22) affect narrow cross-lingual transfer tasks. If cross-lingual transfer across many language pairs is your primary use case, the full-size 311M model is the better choice.

According to recent reports, both models ship with multiple deployment paths for production use. Install the core library with:.

Sentence Transformers (recommended for most users):.

LangChain (pip install langchain-huggingface):.

LlamaIndex (pip install llama-index-embeddings-huggingface):.

According to recent reports, both models also ship with pre-converted ONNX and OpenVINO weights for optimized CPU/accelerator inference, work as embedding endpoints via vLLM (vllm serve ... --task embed), and can be converted to GGUF for Ollama using llama.cpp. See the model cards for full deployment examples.

If you maintain an embedding framework, vector store, or RAG pipeline library and are evaluating these models as a default, here's what you need to know:.

To discuss adopting these models as a default in your project, open an issue at ibm-granite/granite-embedding-models.

Industry observers note that these two multilingual models are part of the broader Granite Embedding R2 family, which also includes two high-performing English-focused models: granite-embedding-english-r2 (149M parameters) and granite-embedding-small-english-r2 (47M parameters). If your data is predominantly English, the English models offer higher retrieval quality on English benchmarks at a smaller footprint, since they don't need to allocate capacity across 200+ languages.

Both models are available now on Hugging Face under the IBM Granite Embedding collection:.

You can try the small models interactively (on CPU) via a Granite Embedding demo here on Hugging Face Spaces, or run the full examples notebook in Google Colab:.

Industry observers note that you can access our detailed technical report covering the full training methodology, per-language evaluations, and pruning ablations here Granite Multilingual Embedding R2 report. For questions, feedback, or concerns, visit ibm-granite/granite-embedding-models on GitHub.

Framework maintainers: If you'd like to adopt these models as a default in your project, open an issue at ibm-granite/granite-embedding-models — we're happy to help with integration, testing, and any questions about licensing or deployment.

#149369. How to change your VPN location in 2026, and what to do when it will not change

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1937 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

How to change your VPN location in 2026, and what to do when it will not change

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the thing every VPN offers is the ability to change the country you seem to be browsing from.
  • In a recent development, then there's a website that detects your actual city.
  • In a recent development, A VPN moves one thing: the address your traffic arrives from.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the thing every VPN offers is the ability to change the country you seem to be browsing from. Choose a country. Connect. On a good day the whole process is under a minute.

In a recent development, then there's a website that detects your actual city. Or maybe a map will drop a pin on your street. Both of those are worth understanding: how to change the location properly, and why something on your phone apparently knows more about where you are.

In a recent development, A VPN moves one thing: the address your traffic arrives from. Your phone still knows which street it is standing on. Your browser still holds whatever it was told last week. Your account still says where you signed up. Those answers can all differ at once, and all be true.

Three locations a website can read, and what a VPN actually moves.

Does a VPN change your IP? Yes. That is almost certainly what was being asked. When you connect to a VPN, your traffic is sent from a server in the selected country. Websites will see an IP address associated with that server, not your IP address over your home internet connection. Based on the information they deduced from your old IP address, they will now deduce information based on your newly introduced IP address.

It has been revealed that what does not change is your device. Your phone still knows its location via mobile masts, Wi-Fi and satellites. Your browser still remembers the permissions you've given. Your accounts still remember which country you signed up in. These are separate systems, and a VPN does not extend into them.

In a recent development, the first three steps change your location. The last three are what most guides leave out, and they are the reason it sticks.

Distance costs speed, so pick the closest country that does the job rather than the most exotic one on the list.

In Senton you open the location list, choose the country and connect. The connection screen then shows which location is live.

Sources indicate that use our what is my IP page. It should now show the country you chose.

A browser that can read your device location will carry on doing so whatever your VPN notes.

Anything excluded from the tunnel still uses your ordinary connection and still shows your ordinary location.

Do step three. Knowing whether your public address actually changed tells you immediately whether this is a VPN problem or one of the other six, and it takes ten seconds.

Step two, on a real phone. The connection screen names the country you are connected through. The address shown is a documentation example, not a live server.

Industry observers note that choose a country that is appropriate for everyday use and stay with it. Most reasons for changing location do not require a specific country. Distance costs speed. Only choose a specific country when the task requires it, such as reaching a service from your home country while you travel. Senton has servers in 50+ countries to pick from.

Three questions settle it in most cases.

Do you need one particular country, or simply a different one?

Does speed matter more here than the country does?

Will you sign in to an account that expects your usual country?

If none of them point at a specific country, take the nearest one and move on.

Step one, on a real phone. The list shows a response time beside each country, which is the quickest way to judge what a location will cost you in speed.

The steps appear the same across all platforms. What varies is what those steps cover. With Android, the app handles the traffic that the system routes to it. With a browser extension, the extension reaches only that browser, and every other program on the machine continues to use your original address. Senton ships an Android app and a Chrome extension today, with iPhone and desktop still to come, and the current list lives on our apps page.

Try testing the connection by itself before you start looking for a problem. Turn off the VPN and check your address, then connect to a server in a country that is obviously different from your own and check again. If you're based in the Gulf, a country such as Germany or the United Kingdom will make this difference very obvious.

If the new address is in the same country as the server you have chosen, and the address has actually changed, then your VPN is working properly. If you then encounter any oddity, it is one of the seven problems listed below, not a connection problem.

Sources indicate that travelling is when most people first notice the mismatch. The connection claims one country, the airport Wi-Fi and the phone in your pocket say another.

According to recent reports, this is where people return to Google. The connection has changed but the page still displays your city. Below are all the possibilities that may occur, in the order in which they most commonly do.

It has been revealed that this is the most commonly encountered one. If you once clicked Allow on the popup that asks whether a site may know your location, you have given that website the geolocation permission, and it can continue to access your device's location instead of deducing it from your address.

On a phone that is more accurate than a location guess based on an IP address. This means that your browser can inform a website that your phone is in Dubai, while you are actually connected to a server in London. Both can indeed be true at once, which is why the website looks as though it has caught you out. Changing servers does not revoke any permissions you have already granted.

One tap on Allow, months ago, and the site no longer has to guess from your address at all.

An IP address is just one piece of the puzzle. Location on a mobile phone can be determined using satellite data, nearby Wi-Fi routers, mobile masts and also location sensors within the phone itself. This system is completely unaware of which country your data leaves from when you use a VPN. As a result, a location service can still determine your position even though your connection may seem to be originating from a different country.

This is more apparent with apps than with browsers. Location permission for an app is requested by the app from the operating system independently of the VPN. Thus, an app granted months ago will continue to report your true location.

Satellites, Wi-Fi hotspots and mobile masts put your phone on this street corner. None of them ask which country your VPN traffic leaves from.

Now imagine that you visit an online store based in the UAE and choose that location as your region. If you then return later from a German IP address, you might still see the UAE storefront. This is because your saved region preference is more specific than an inference made from your address, and switching IP addresses does not cause previously saved preferences to be removed from your browser. A private window would resolve this immediately.

Signing in gives a service far more than a lookup by address. A user account can remember the country associated with the profile, the card used to pay for it, the region of the app store where it was created, previous shipping addresses, and all previous sign-in locations.

Industry observers note that most services tend to place more value on that history than on whatever your connection claims today. Google does this with its search results, which can use past activity and location information from a user's device as well as the address in front of it. A latest address does not eliminate this information, which is why you may see a different version of the same site when you are signed out compared to when you are signed in.

There is also a less obvious possibility. Your VPN may have changed your address correctly, but the site then looked up that address in a database that disagrees. No one physically locates an address. Instead, sites query a commercial database. These databases vary from one another and also go out of date, a point Cloudflare makes plainly about geolocation.

Recent findings suggest that none of that means your own address leaked. If step three showed the right country, the connection is fine and the database is wrong.

According to recent reports, some apps do benefit from being sent outside the tunnel. It can also be a very effective method of confusing yourself. Anything you exclude will continue to use your usual connection and report your usual position.

Senton's Bypasser works this way. Traffic routed around the tunnel goes out normally. If one app detects your VPN country and another detects your actual country, recheck your bypass settings before blaming the connection.

Anything listed here connects directly instead of through the tunnel. Useful, and also why one app can show your real location while another reveals your VPN country.

Asked of the phone, not the VPN.

Recent findings suggest that each one says something minimal on its own. In combination, however, the inconsistencies stand out: a UK address, a time zone from the Gulf, a UAE account, and finally the browser naming Dubai. None of that was deduced by breaking encryption. It was all available in the signals.

Most of the time, not. A VPN only alters your location by address, and your actual device location remains unchanged. Which is why switching to a different country may have no impact in an app that already has permission to access your location, and why using only a VPN will not move you on a map, in find-my-device functionality on a phone, or in a family location-sharing app.

On supported Android devices, Senton does this separately through Geo-Spoofing. If the app is granted Android's mock-location permission, the location reported to supported apps can be set to match the country of the VPN you are using. This relies on the app and the platform. Some apps will reject mock location information or use other signals. It has no effect on your actual location, the country associated with your account or your payment information.

Geo-Spoofing is not a switch you simply flip. Android requires you to nominate the app as its mock location source first, which is a deliberate barrier.

It doesn't affect the rules you are subject to. Using a VPN is lawful in most countries, although a few restrict it, which we cover in our guide on whether VPNs are legal. Again, a service may have its own terms. Many platforms restrict the actions you can take from a foreign country, and changing countries does not affect those restrictions. What we do and do not keep is set out on our no-logs policy page.

If there is to be one thing taken away from this article, let it be this. A VPN alters the location associated with your internet connection. Everything else, from satellite positioning and Wi-Fi scanning to browser permissions, account settings and stored data, remains the same.

Sources indicate that just because you can see your actual city somewhere doesn't necessarily mean your VPN didn't work. First check your public address. Then figure out what other signal the site is picking up, and whether you'd like to continue sending that signal.

#149365. Bonooru Devlog #3: The PC takes the wheel

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2752 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Bonooru Devlog #3: The PC takes the wheel

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that ode to Joy now plays on the Switch 2 from the PC: a command on my Mac, my own bridge firmware, my own controller firmware, every note right.
  • Recent findings suggest that bonooru is my side project to play arbitrary melodies on the ocarina in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2.
  • Every box is mine now, except the console.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ode to Joy now plays on the Switch 2 from the PC: a command on my Mac, my own bridge firmware, my own controller firmware, every note right. And if I yank the bridge out mid-song, the controller lets go of every button in about 20 ms at worst, and it measured that itself.

Recent findings suggest that bonooru is my side project to play arbitrary melodies on the ocarina in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2. It does that by pretending to be a wired controller. The chain is a desktop app on the PC, a "bridge" RP2040 board on USB, a UART link, and a "controller" RP2040 board that the Switch 2 sees as a Pro Controller. Devlog #0 explains the idea, Devlog #1 measures the ocarina, Devlog #2 is the controller firmware.

The Bonooru chain after Epic 3. Every box is mine now, except the console.

Industry observers note that at the end of Epic 2 the controller board was mine: it enumerated as a wired Pro Controller and played a melody baked into its own firmware. But the PC only sent HELLO and START, and the bridge board still ran knflrpn's 2wiCC_Comms, which copies bytes between USB and UART with no idea of what a frame is.

The goal of Epic 3 was milestone M4: the PC drives the controller through the bridge. That meant three fresh pieces of software and one question:.

Five stories, five PRs (#31 to #35), plus the retrospective (#36), from 24 to 26 November.

Like in Epic 2, the order wasn't the obvious one. The two stories that need no hardware went first: the Rust codec (3.2) and the link session (3.3). Then the bridge firmware (3.1), then the end-to-end tool (3.4), then the fail-safe measurements (3.5). By the time anything Rust touched a serial port, it had been tested for a day against a fake controller.

It has been revealed that story 3.2 (PR #31) started the app/ Cargo workspace, pinned to Rust 1.100.0, with one library crate: ocb-core. Its protocol module is the Rust twin of the C library from Devlog #2: COBS, CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE, frame encode and decode in the same receive order, every message type, the 8-byte controller state.

Two rules make this crate what it is:.

The point of the C library's 239 text vectors in 7 files was exactly this moment: a second implementation in another language. The Rust test reads all seven files and must pass every case, and checks that its PROTO_VERSION matches the vector headers. proptest round-trips COBS, frames, the receive splitter and messages on random input, and checks that no decoder panics on arbitrary bytes. CI runs it all on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS, with clippy -D warnings and a cargo-deny licence check.

Recent findings suggest that the code review had an interesting result. One reviewer compared the Rust codec with the C one on about 100,000 generated inputs: COBS, frame decoding, the splitter's events and counters, the message length rules. No difference. Every vital finding was in the test gates, not in the codec. The purity gate, for example, was a text search that use std as s, std :: fs or a path split over two lines walked straight past. It now scans a token stream, and each of its 34 bad fixtures names the exact hit it must produce.

That's a theme for the whole epic, so I'll say it once here: a test that can't fail is worse than no test, because it tells you something is checked when it isn't.

Story 3.3 (PR #32) is the part I'm proudest of, and you can't see it on any screen.

In a recent development, the link protocol has rules: a session opens with HELLO until the controller answers INFO; events are sent go-back-N with cumulative ACKs and a 50 ms resend; the app may only send as many QUEUE_EVENTs as the controller has room for (credits from STATUS.free); a semantic NAK abandons the piece; a mid-session NAK VERSION means the controller rebooted. All of that lives in ocb_core::link::Session, and the session never touches a port or a clock. It takes bytes and a time, and gives back bytes, events and the next time it wants to be called. It's the sans-IO style of quinn-proto, the QUIC library that keeps its protocol logic separate from any socket.

Sans-IO: the session is pure logic; the adapter owns the port and the clock.

In a recent development, because the session is pure, it can be tested with a fake clock against a fake controller, deterministically, thousands of times. That fake controller is its own dev-only crate, ocb-sim, with an impaired channel that drops, corrupts, duplicates, reorders and injects junk. One sample run, 2000 events through a controller queue of only 5 slots, with every impairment at 10 %:.

Every event arrived exactly once, in order, in every run.

All tests green, then the code review found nine key bugs, and reproduced most of them with scratch tests. Two of my favourites:.

And the finding that explains the others: the simulator was kinder than the firmware. The test driver read the session's own counters to check the session, called its timers every millisecond whatever it asked for, and the fake controller answered more politely than the real one does. So the driver now checks invariants from the wire only, decodes every byte the session sends, keeps strict timers, reorders across steps, and the fake controller copies the firmware's TX priority, its reply rings and its fallbacks. Each fix has a regression test that fails on the old code.

Story 3.1 (PR #33) replaced 2wiCC_Comms with my bridge firmware. It's split like the controller: a pure C core (bridge/core, testable on the PC, loadable from Python) and a thin platform layer with TinyUSB and the UART. One core, one non-blocking super-loop. No code path is allowed to block.

"Ahead of queued app frames" doesn't mean "instantly". A due heartbeat still waits for the frame in flight, whatever is already in the UART's software ring, the 32-byte hardware FIFO and the shift register. The controller declares the link dead after 80 ms of silence, but the protocol promises a gap of at most 27 ms between heartbeats. At 460800 baud a byte takes about 21.7 µs, so every byte allowed to wait in front adds up.

Recent findings suggest that my first limit, 16 bytes ahead in the software ring, left a margin of 0.25 ms and nothing to stop someone from raising it. The review made it 8 bytes, and the build now refuses any value that could break 27 ms:.

firmware/bridge/core/bridge.c: a negative array size is a compile error.

The host test (F.7) runs 23 bursts of 512 maximum-size frames with a fake clock and measures every heartbeat gap: 17.36 to 23.07 ms, limit 27. Its first version passed for the wrong reason. The model rounded every character to the clock's 5 µs step (25 µs instead of 21.7), and a heartbeat plus three maximum frames then took exactly 800 characters, 20.000 ms. Every gap read 20.000 ms and the worst case was never exercised. Exact character times fixed it, and the test now also requires a gap above 20.5 ms, so it can't pass vacuously again.

In a recent development, two boards, two USB cables, and a UART between them. Either can be powered first, and a board must never push current into an unpowered neighbour through its TX pin. The controller's side of that rule (TX high-impedance until RX idles high) is in Devlog #2. Story 3.1 added the bridge's side, the probe:.

Industry observers note that the bridge's probe (AD-20). No heartbeat while probing: TX is not driven.

The review found that my first version, on a link loss, started the next pulse in the same step: TX never actually went high-impedance, and the leftovers of the cut frame were still sent. Now a loss releases TX at once, empties the ring and waits 10 ms so the controller sees a break and releases too. And every link-up starts with a lone 0x00, which ends any half frame the controller's receiver might still hold.

Sources indicate that one surprise, and not from the firmware: macOS completes the Pro Controller handshake by itself. With the controller plugged into my Mac, STATUS noted console_ready 1 with no probe script running. My bench command expected "not ready" and printed one FAIL, with exactly the right replies for a ready console. The Epic 2 retrospective had already written that fact down; the H-row hadn't caught up. Now every bench row states which host the controller is plugged into.

Story 3.4 (PR #34) is a small command-line tool, ocb-dev, the first real user of the session. It takes exactly two arguments, a serial port and a timeline file, and it's the first form of the serial worker the real app will have in Epic 4.

The timeline is the same Ode to Joy the controller played from its own memory in Devlog #2: 62 notes, 158 events, generated from the ocarina profile measured in Epic 1. Same melody, so the comparison is fair; the only difference is that now every event crosses the wire from the PC.

Sources indicate that the tool is the adapter from the sans-IO diagram. Its loop sleeps until the session's next timeout, a deadline or incoming bytes, then feeds the session and drains it:.

app/tools/ocb-dev/src/runner/mod.rs, trimmed.

According to recent reports, the runner is generic over the port, the clock and "the owner" (me, pressing Enter). The bench uses a real serial port and a real clock; the dry run plugs the same runner into ocb-sim with a fake clock and a scripted owner. Same code, two worlds.

One ocb-dev melody run (simplified).

B forwards every frame and adds its own HEARTBEAT every 20 ms; it's left out of the arrows to keep the picture readable.

The "first input" step is a lesson from Devlog #2: the Switch 2 doesn't show a wired controller until it gets an input. The tool presses D-pad down three times (never A, which could launch something), then asks me to dismiss the game's controller screen and reopen the ocarina, keeps the link alive with PING, and starts only when I press Enter.

The Epic 2 retrospective left one action, #27, that I took seriously: before any bench session, review the bench tools and the commands of every bench row, and dry-run every new or changed tool against the simulated model. Half of Epic 2's failures had been my own test scripts, at the Switch, with the console in my hands.

Sources indicate that for ocb-dev the code review found twelve important concerns, and the dry run made each one a failing test before the fix. Two would have wasted a bench session:.

The M4 exit criterion was a soak: 10 minutes at 460800 baud without losing a byte, or else evaluate 921600. ocb-dev soak streams one event per millisecond, about 100 times the rate of a melody, with states harmless on any host. It runs with the controller on the Mac, on the debug build that exposes the controller's counters.

Sources indicate that 600,000 events, zero bytes lost, zero transport NAKs. 921600 baud isn't needed. The only bench bug was cosmetic: the summary line printed frames sent 0, because the session restarts its counters at every STOP. Fixed after the bench, with a test that failed on the old code.

Story 3.5 (PR #35) had no latest feature. It was the one I cared about most: can I trust these boards with my console? The requirement: when the link dies mid-song, the console must see nothing pressed within 100 ms, every time.

ocb-dev got two more keyword modes: failsafe plays the melody in rounds and waits for me to break the link in each one; watch follows the console's state while I put it through sleep and settings changes.

The review found something uncomfortable: two numbers in the acceptance criteria could not be measured with what the controller exposed.

My original plan had been "no firmware change, the design already bounds it". At the review I changed my mind and added a measurement to the controller instead: a 5-byte debug STATUS v5 block, debug builds only, no wire or protocol version change.

The lesson went straight into the retrospective: for every number in an acceptance criterion, the story names the tool and the field that will measure it when the story is written, not at the code review.

Recent findings suggest that the routine, 40 times: the tool prints ROUND n/20: playing, I unplug the bridge's USB (first run) or pull the bridge-TX → controller-RX jumper (second run) in the middle of the melody, listen, plug it back. The next round starts 3 s after the controller is ready again.

According to recent reports, limit 100 ms; worst case 20.02 ms. Every loss was a break (an unplugged RX line, pulled down, reads as one), so the watchdog didn't wait for the 80 ms heartbeat timeout: it acted at once. The number it reports is the time since the last heartbeat, which is why the range sits between 0 and one heartbeat period. And I heard the melody stop at once, in every one of the 40 rounds.

With the multimeter, the controller's TX pin (GP0) read 0.09 V with the bridge unplugged and 0 V with the wire out: the controller releases TX after a loss. My first reading stated 1.41 V, which gave me a moment, until I noticed I had the probe on GP1, the controller's RX, not GP0. And H.1's last part: bridge unpowered, controller in the console, bridge GP1 at 0.26 V (a floating line) and bridge 3V3 at 0 V. No back-powering, in either direction.

The first unplug run had one failed round, and it was the right kind of failure: the melody ended while I was still reading the instructions, so there was no loss to measure. The tool failed that round alone and moved on, as designed. One extra round made it 20.

A.3: worst measured vs limit, and the other margins of this epic (ms).

console_ready is the controller's opinion of whether the console is listening: 1 after the handshake, back to 0 when the console stops polling for more than 100 ms. The app will use it to enable or disable Play. The watch run, one action at a time:.

H.3 on the Switch 2, as the session saw it.

The UX spec had two open questions waiting for exactly these numbers:.

According to recent reports, nothing in the firmware surprised me in this session. The console and my tools did:.

I plan and build Bonooru with the BMad Method and AI agents (Claude). Each story gets a file with its acceptance criteria and every open decision recorded; an agent implements it, three fresh-context reviewers attack it in parallel (one blind, one hunting edge cases, one checking every acceptance criterion), and the findings are fixed or recorded. In this epic that was 9, 11, 12 and 14 notable findings fixed in Stories 3.3, 3.1, 3.4 and 3.5, all before the bench. What needs hardware is mine: I unplugged, pulled wires, held the multimeter and listened to 40 rounds of Ode to Joy being cut short; the agent wrote the tools and recorded the numbers as measured, failed runs included.

In a recent development, epic 3 is 5 story PRs plus the retrospective. At the end, the repo has 44 firmware host tests (ctest, under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer) and 105 Rust tests across ocb-core, ocb-sim and ocb-dev, green on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS. The rules, decisions and bench numbers live in docs/link-protocol.md and docs/test-proposal.md.

Everything so far happens in a terminal. Next epic, Bonooru gets a window: the app finds the bridge by itself, reveals the state of the link as it changes, and lets me move Link with a gamepad on the screen.

In Epic 2 the controller played a melody it carried in its own memory. Now the PC sends every note, and I've pulled the plug 40 times to make sure it lets go.

PaddleOCR 3.5 brings OCR and document parsing tasks closer to the Hugging Face ecosystem. With this release, supported PaddleOCR models can run with Hugging Face Transformers as an inference backend by setting:.

PaddleOCR continues to provide OCR model series such as PP-OCRv5 and document parsing model series such as PaddleOCR-VL 1.5, while Transformers becomes one of the supported backends for running them.

Try the live demo on Hugging Face Spaces: https://huggingface.co/spaces/PaddlePaddle/paddleocr-3.5-transformers-demo.

PaddleOCR 3.5 introduces a more flexible inference-engine interface. Developers can select the backend through the engine parameter and pass backend-specific options through engine_config.

A simple way to understand the stack:.

In a recent development, this release is mainly about the inference backend layer: PaddleOCR continues to provide OCR and document parsing capabilities, while Transformers gives supported PaddleOCR models another backend option that fits naturally into Hugging Face-centered environments. The larger Document AI workflow remains in the hands of developers and application builders.

For RAG, Document AI, and document agent applications, the hard part often starts before the LLM.

In a recent development, developers first need to turn PDFs, scanned documents, screenshots, tables, charts, formulas, and complex page layouts into reliable structured data. If this ingestion step is weak, the downstream LLM workflow may miss key information, retrieve the wrong context, or produce unreliable answers.

PaddleOCR helps address this document ingestion challenge by providing OCR series models such as PP-OCRv5 and document parsing series models such as PaddleOCR-VL-1.5.

It has been revealed that with PaddleOCR 3.5, these capabilities are now easier to connect with Transformers-centered stacks. Supported PaddleOCR models can run with a Transformers backend, while PaddleOCR continues to manage the OCR or document parsing pipeline behind the scenes.

For developers, this means less integration friction and a more natural path from documents to downstream RAG, agent, search, analytics, or automation workflows.

Install PaddleOCR 3.5, PaddleX, Transformers, and a compatible PyTorch build for your hardware.

For example, on a CUDA 12.6 environment:.

For CPU, ROCm, or other environments, install the PyTorch build that matches your target hardware.

The Hugging Face Space uses float32 for broad compatibility. For your own hardware, you can tune backend-specific options through engine_config:.

The best configuration depends on your model, hardware, and deployment environment.

Use the Transformers backend when you want PaddleOCR’s OCR and document parsing capabilities to fit more naturally into a Hugging Face-centered stack.

This is especially useful if you are building RAG, Document AI, search, analytics, or agent applications and already rely on PyTorch / Transformers infrastructure for model loading, experimentation, deployment, or model artifact management.

The Transformers backend is a good fit when you want:.

When maximizing OCR or document parsing throughput is the priority, PaddleOCR’s default paddle_static backend is usually the recommended choice.

Recent findings suggest that this release is not about replacing one backend with another. It is about giving developers more flexibility: use PaddleOCR for OCR and document parsing capabilities, and choose the inference backend that best fits your stack.

Terminal vs GUI for Server Management: When Each One Wins

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for server management, pick the terminal or a GUI by task, not by habit.
  • Below: how each works, a task table, and 7 example tools.
  • According to recent reports, your ssh client opens one encrypted connection, asks the server for a shell, sends your keystrokes and gets text back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for server management, pick the terminal or a GUI by task, not by habit. The plain terminal is best for small, quick tasks and needs no third-party app. A GUI is best for browsing files and handling several servers in tabs. Some GUI apps, like Termius and CtrlOps, also run saved scripts.

Below: how each works, a task table, and 7 example tools.

I made a short video on the same question:.

According to recent reports, your ssh client opens one encrypted connection, asks the server for a shell, sends your keystrokes and gets text back. For your session, the server starts only your shell and the commands you run, next to the SSH service.

In a recent development, inside that connection, SSH uses channels. RFC 4254, the SSH connection standard from 2006, claims: "All terminal sessions, forwarded connections, etc., are channels." It adds: "Multiple channels are multiplexed into a single connection." A channel can ask for an interactive shell or for one command:.

In this post, web1, db1 and the other host names are example aliases from ~/.ssh/config on your computer:.

It has been revealed that A GUI SSH client uses the same SSH protocol and server account as the ssh command. It opens more channels for you: a shell per terminal tab, short commands that read things like disk use, and, in most file browsers, SFTP.

SFTP itself is part of SSH: on OpenSSH servers, sshd starts sftp-server through its Subsystem option.

Sources indicate that the Termius docs, for example, say that for autocomplete it "opens additional exec channels next to the main shell channel". In CtrlOps, gauges for CPU, RAM and disk show "the numbers top, free -h and df -h / give you, without running them".

CtrlOps reads them "over the SSH you already use" (Infra Monitoring).

According to recent reports, so the SSH GUI vs command line choice is not about access: a GUI client does not unlock anything the terminal cannot do. It types the commands for you and shows the answer as a list or a gauge. It needs no fresh port on the server, because it uses the SSH service already running.

A web panel runs on the server itself: a service, a port and a login page that you open in a browser.

Recent findings suggest that by default, Cockpit listens on port 9090 (Running Cockpit) and "uses your system's normal user logins and privileges" (Cockpit). Thanks to systemd socket activation, it runs only on demand. Webmin listens on port 10000 by default, and its docs say it "runs with full root privileges" (Webmin docs).

So each panel is one more service per server, to keep updated and open only to you, for example through a VPN.

Sources indicate that planning to manage a second server from Cockpit? That feature "is deprecated as of Cockpit 322" (Cockpit docs). It is off by default on newer releases such as Fedora 41, RHEL 10 and CentOS Stream 10 (Cockpit 322 notes).

Usually no. Keep the server text-only and run the GUI on your own computer.

A GUI for a Linux server can run in three places. Two are on the server: a desktop or a web panel. The third is an app on your own computer that connects over SSH.

There is no Ubuntu Server GUI by default: the server image "will not install a graphical user interface" (Ubuntu 26.04).

RHEL differs: "By default, the Server with GUI base environment is selected" (RHEL 9 docs), so pick Server or Minimal Install there.

Sources indicate that A desktop costs memory. Ubuntu Desktop 26.04.1 LTS asks for 6 GB of RAM (download page). The Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS installer needs 1.5 GB (requirements). The versions differ, but the gap is clear.

Recent findings suggest that A desktop also adds packages to patch. A STIG is a security checklist from DISA, the US Defense Information Systems Agency. The RHEL 9 STIG (v2r8, rule RHEL-09-215070) states: "A graphical display manager must not be installed on RHEL 9 unless approved.".

Sources indicate that A desktop can make sense on a home lab server, or for one GUI-only app (see the X11 question in the FAQ). To make a server with a desktop boot to text mode:.

Check it with systemctl get-default, which should now print multi-user.target.

To undo it, run sudo systemctl set-default graphical.target.

Typing df -h answers "is the disk full?" in one line, and grep -rn "server_name" /etc/nginx/ finds the right config file. But when you do not know a file's name, seeing the folder beats guessing paths.

Tech Report: The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

Introducing the Ettin Reranker Family

📅 19 May 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face
