📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.

The reason is that people tend to see more of their own qualities in others.

The generous person sees others as generous and the selfish person sees others as selfish.

Dr Dustin Wood, the study’s first author, said:.

“A huge suite of negative personality traits are associated with viewing others negatively.

The simple tendency to see people negatively indicates a greater likelihood of depression and various personality disorders.”.

The conclusions come from a series of three studies.

In one people were asked to judge the positive and negative characteristics of three other people.

The more positively they judged those people, the more happy, enthusiastic, capable and emotionally stable they turned out to be themselves.

People who judged others more positively also turned out to be more satisfied with their own lives.

Set against this, those who judged others more negatively had higher levels of narcissism and antisocial behaviour.

The researchers even returned to the same people a year later and found the results were the same.

This suggests that what people’s ratings of others say about themselves remains stable over time.

Personality disorders are often diagnosed at least partly by how people view others, the authors write:.

“…although narcissists may perceive others as being uninteresting or worthless, this may not reflect how they see themselves.

Similarly, individuals displaying behaviors typical of paranoid personality disorder may believe that others are malevolent and untrustworthy, even though they may not see themselves that way.

Machiavellianism is usually measured in part by asking individuals the extent to which they perceive a lack of sincerity, integrity, or selflessness in others’ actions, and narcissistic behavior is thought to be prompted in part by a belief that other people are inferior, uninteresting, and unworthy of attention.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Wood et al., 2010).

Sources indicate that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

We are two founders in India who kept opening food apps late at night without being hungry. So we built the ritual without the spend.

Pretend restaurants and menus, a cart, and a full bill with delivery, platform fee and taxes. It asks what is making you order: stress, boredom, habit and so on. A pretend rider on a map with a timer. It charges Rs 0, because nothing is sent. A journal keeps a note of what set the urge off.

It is a free Android app built with React and Capacitor, and there is a browser demo that takes about 30 seconds: https://try.feedmenot.co.in/.

What we do not know yet is whether it changes how people order in real life. We are early.

What would you change about the first 30 seconds?

Drafted with an AI assistant for the FeedMeNot founders.

Shipping a Trillion Parameters With a Hub Bucket: Delta Weight Sync in TRL

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR, because you have models to train and we respect that:.
  • If you read our previous post on the landscape of async RL training, you already know the punchline.
  • According to recent reports, the inference engine speaks the policy of step N.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR, because you have models to train and we respect that:.

Async RL just got a lot cheaper. Read on.

If you read our previous post on the landscape of async RL training, you already know the punchline. Every async RL library, regardless of how it spells "actor model" or which color its NCCL backend is painted, eventually trips over the same root: weight synchronization.

According to recent reports, the inference engine speaks the policy of step N. The trainer just finished step N+1. The fresh weights have to get from one side to the other before the inference engine starts drifting hopelessly off-policy. This sits on the critical path whether you are running sync or async: a blocking transfer is wasted idle compute of GPUs not generating tokens. With a sparse delta path you collapse that idle time into seconds, and the trainer does not even have to wait for the inference engine to be ready: it just publishes "weights ready" and uploads the weights to the shared bucket the moment its optimizer step finishes, while the inference engine fetches on its own time.

Sources indicate that fireworks put a very memorable number on this in their post Frontier RL Is Cheaper Than You Think: for a frontier 1T-parameter checkpoint at fp8 (their setting), a full snapshot is 1024 GiB, and that is what conventional wisdom says you have to ship every time you update your rollout fleet. That is the kind of number that gets people to start drawing diagrams with mega-clusters, RDMA fabrics, and dedicated cross-region links. Their measured average delta between adjacent checkpoints lands at 20.3 GiB, or 1.98% of the full model, and "more than 98% of weights in bf16 format remain bit-equivalent between consecutive checkpoints".

According to recent reports, cursor's Composer 2 report tells a parallel story. They run training and inference in different regions and stitch them together with a shared S3 bucket (their exact words), into which the trainer uploads compressed weight diffs every training step. Each cluster independently downloads and reconstructs from the shared delta chain, "requiring no direct connectivity to the training cluster". The two sides never speak to each other about parameters directly. The bucket is the wire.

Both papers agree on three things, and we want to repeat them slowly, because the rest of this post is essentially a faithful open source translation:.

In a recent development, the only thing missing was a version of this story that you can pip install. So we wrote one.

Before we wire anything up, it is worth understanding why this whole game is even winnable. The "98% of weights do not change" claim sounds suspiciously like one of those numbers that works in the demo and falls apart in the wild. It is not. It falls out of how bf16 arithmetic works at the learning rates RL uses.

A bf16 number has 7 mantissa bits. Between two consecutive powers of two, there are exactly 27=1282^7 = 12827=128 representable values, so the spacing between adjacent bf16 numbers around ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ is roughly ∣w∣⋅2−7|w| \cdot 2^{-7}∣w∣⋅2−7. An revision gets absorbed by the bf16 cast whenever it sits below half of that spacing, i.e., when ∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256|\Delta w| < |w|/256∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256. This is the "bf16 visibility threshold" PULSE plots in their Figure 3.

Now look at what Adam does. At an RL learning rate of, say, 3×10−63 \times 10^{-6}3×10−6, the patch to a single weight is: Δw=−η⋅m^v^+ϵ\Delta w = -\eta \cdot \frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}} + \epsilon}Δw=−η⋅v^​+ϵm^​.

The normalized step m^/(v^+ϵ)\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)m^/(v^​+ϵ) is roughly order one, so ∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6|\Delta w| \approx \eta \approx 3 \times 10^{-6}∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6. For most weights, ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ sits somewhere around 10−210^{-2}10−2 to 10−110^{-1}10−1 (PULSE reports a median of 0.019 for representative LLM weights). The threshold ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256 at that magnitude is around 4×10−54 \times 10^{-5}4×10−5 to 4×10−44 \times 10^{-4}4×10−4, which is bigger than the revision.

Sources indicate that in other words: the optimizer is whispering, and bf16 cannot hear it. The patch gets absorbed by rounding, the byte representation of www does not change, and from the inference engine's perspective, this weight did not move. Multiply that by a few hundred million parameters, and you get the >99% sparsity number, for free, with zero approximation.

This is exactly the argument made formal in the PULSE paper (Mihai & Belilovsky, 2026). They define two thresholds. The absorption bound 10η10\eta10η is the conservative worst case for an Adam update, and the effective bound η\etaη is the regime you actually live in. The bf16 visibility threshold is ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256. Whenever the update sits below the visibility threshold, it gets absorbed, and the bf16 byte does not change. Their Figure 3 plots both bounds against a cloud of representative LLM weights, and the conclusion is unambiguous: at η=3×10−6\eta = 3 \times 10^{-6}η=3×10−6, the absorption bound itself already sits below the visibility threshold for almost every weight in the model. They measure this empirically across Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B), Llama-3.2-3B, and Gemma-3-4B, and consistently find a mean per-step sparsity of ~99%, with a standard deviation of 0.2 to 0.4% over 400 training steps. The worst-case step stays above 98%. So <1% changed is not a lucky measurement; it is what the arithmetic guarantees.

It has been revealed that we do not have to predict this analytically (and indeed, we tried predicting the change mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, but recall was a sad 30%, more on that later). We just need to observe which bytes flipped. That is a tiny boolean tensor per parameter, computed right around the optimizer step.

Here is where the second piece of the story comes in, and where this post stops being a translation of Fireworks/Cursor and starts being a Hugging Face thing.

It has been revealed that A Bucket is a repo type on the Hub designed for high-frequency object storage. No commit ceremony, no PR workflow, no LFS quirks. You add files, you list files, you download files. The Python interface is two functions:.

Recent findings suggest that that is it. Two function calls and your weights are in flight.

Recent findings suggest that under the hood, buckets are backed by Xet, the Hub's content-defined chunking storage layer. Xet looks at every file you upload, slices it into chunks based on its actual content (not fixed offsets), and deduplicates against everything already in the bucket. The practical upshot, which is delightful in this context, is that even if we were too lazy to write the sparse encoding and just uploaded full anchors every step, Xet would still only transfer the changed chunks. Sparse encoding + Xet stack: we pay for what moved, and we pay for it once.

This is the open source equivalent of the "shared S3 bucket" both Fireworks and Cursor reach for, except the storage layer already knows about content hashing, your existing HF token already has permission, and it composes natively with the rest of the stack (Spaces, datasets, models).

The full architecture has exactly three boxes and one shared substrate:.

The property to internalize, the one Cursor's paper sells hard and that holds verbatim here: the trainer and the rollout server never talk to each other about weights. They exchange a tiny POST containing {"repo_id": ..., "filename": ...}, and that is the entire control plane. The actual byte transfer happens between each side and the bucket, in parallel, with no shared network fabric.

Industry observers note that the trainer writes. Replicas read. The Hub does the plumbing.

It has been revealed that now we can open the hood. The protocol has four parts: a wire format, a bucket layout, a 30 line vLLM extension, and a trainer side change detector. It is honestly less code than it sounds.

Sources indicate that we picked safetensors for the on-disk and on-wire format. It is already the canonical checkpoint format on the Hub, every reasonable framework can read it, and the header carries arbitrary string metadata. That metadata field is where we hide the protocol.

There are two kinds of files in the bucket.

Anchors look like a normal checkpoint: one tensor per parameter, full bf16 weights, written every NNN syncs (we default to N=10N=10N=10).

Deltas are the interesting bit. For each parameter that actually changed, we store two entries: a flat int32 tensor of element indices, and a bf16 tensor of values at those indices.

A few nice consequences of this choice:.

According to recent reports, the cadence is straightforward: anchor every Nth step, delta in between. Both end up in the same bucket under anchors/ and deltas/ prefixes. Each newly introduced inference replica only needs to grab the most recent anchor and then replay the deltas since.

The trainer needs to know which bf16 elements actually flipped. We do this with a tiny BF16ChangeDetector that registers a pre-step and post-step hook on the optimizer:.

The actual code in the PR has a bit more plumbing (matching optimizer param objects to model params via data_ptr(), because Accelerate wraps them as different Python objects), but the idea fits on a napkin: snapshot, step, diff.

Sources indicate that this is ground truth. We tried the more elegant path of predicting the mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, using the bf16 ULP threshold directly. It works in principle. In practice, recall was around 30%, which means we would have shipped a delta missing two thirds of the actual updates. Adam's normalization is messy enough that the analytical threshold is not tight. So we just compare bytes. It costs one bf16 CPU snapshot of the model on the trainer side, which we are willing to pay.

The four phases of the newly introduced _sync_weight flow are:.

The line that matters is the parenthesis. Inference was paused for 1.1 seconds. The remaining 9.4 seconds were spent uploading, which occurred while the rollout server was still generating tokens. With NCCL, we were paying the full sync time as pause time. Here we are paying for it as background time.

It has been revealed that vLLM has a clean abstraction for this called WeightTransferEngine. We implement a DeltaWeightTransferEngine whose receive_weights method is, in spirit:.

We register it via vLLM's --worker-extension-cls flag, which means no fork of vLLM is required. You install TRL into the same image as vLLM, point the CLI at our class, and you are done.

It has been revealed that worth mentioning: vLLM itself has an in-flight effort to land sparse weight transfer natively, vllm-project/vllm#40096. It adds receive_sparse_weights() and trainer_send_sparse_weights() directly on the WeightTransferEngine base class, with patches encoded as (indices, values) and applied in place via index_copy_(), removing the GPU/CPU validation roundtrip entirely. The PR reports a transfer of 0.16 MB in 0.40 ms for a sparse patch on Qwen3-1.7B versus 942 MB in 192 ms for a full dense send.

One honest caveat in our implementation on the inference side: we keep a CPU bf16 snapshot of the model so we can reconstruct full tensors from sparse (indices, values) patches, because load_weights in vLLM today expects full tensors. Once #40096 (or its successor) lands and exposes an in-place sparse load_weights path, we can apply the indices directly on the GPU and drop the snapshot!

Industry observers note that this is the part we are smug about. Everything we have described so far works on your laptop, but the point of routing weights through a Hub bucket is that the trainer and the rollout server do not have to live anywhere near each other. So we ran a fully disaggregated training with three machines, none of which share a network:.

Sources indicate that setting this up is genuinely a few hf CLI calls. The vLLM Space's Dockerfile is essentially the upstream vLLM image plus pip install trl@... plus the entrypoint:.

And kick off training from anywhere on the planet that can talk HTTPS:.

Recent findings suggest that the trainer never opens a port. The Space never sees the trainer's IP. The Wordle environment does not know either of them exists. They all talk to the Hub. Training converged on the immediate-EOS sanity check, then on real Wordle rollouts: reward went up, delta payloads stayed in the 20 to 35 MB band, and the inference-paused window per sync stayed around a second. The full run logs are linked in the companion PR.

A few things, and we think they are massive.

In a recent development, async RL training without a cluster. If you have one GPU and a Hugging Face account, you can now do real disaggregated training. Your trainer is on the GPU; your rollout fleet lives in Spaces; your environment lives in another Space; weights move through a bucket. This used to require either a colocated setup (with all the throughput compromises that brings) or a real cluster with shared networking. It does not anymore.

Sources indicate that multi-replica inference, for free. Stand up two vLLM Spaces, or ten. They all pull from the same bucket. Xet content-addresses storage so consecutive anchors share chunks at rest (which keeps your bucket from blowing up), and the Hub's edge cache makes repeated downloads of the same file cheap to serve. Want a globally distributed rollout fleet? That is now a small DevOps exercise, not a research project.

Recent findings suggest that A wire format you can debug with your existing tools. A delta is a safetensors file. You can safe_open it from a notebook, list its keys, inspect the indices, compute the sparsity yourself. We have spent enough hours in tcpdump on opaque NCCL streams to appreciate this.

Sources indicate that A path to frontier scale. The 20 to 35 MB number is for Qwen3-0.6B. The interesting question is what the curve looks like once you turn the dial up. Let us do the napkin math.

Take Llama-3.1-405B. In bf16 that is 810 GB on disk. PULSE measures ~99% mean per-step sparsity at RL learning rates, so the actual delta sits around 1% of the parameters. Their deployment-measured encoding hits 108 MB on a 7B model, which is the ~130× reduction PULSE reports. Scaled linearly to 405B, the delta lands at roughly 6 GB per step.

It has been revealed that what does that buy you in wall-clock? NCCL is fast inside a cluster, sure. Assume a generous 100 GB/s aggregate broadcast bandwidth (multi-node, RDMA, the works). A full sync is 810 GB / 100 GB/s ≈ 8 seconds of inference pause, every step. With the delta path, the trainer streams 6 GB to a bucket in the background while generation keeps running, and the rollout server's actual paused window is just the apply step, which on this scale lands at a couple of seconds. So even before we leave the cluster, delta cuts the visible pause by 4× and the bytes on the wire by ~130×.

It has been revealed that now leave the cluster. NCCL straight up does not work across clouds. Once you want a rollout fleet in us-east, another in eu-west, maybe one in a Hugging Face Space, the bucket-based path is the only path. At 1 GB/s of usable internet bandwidth, a single full broadcast would take 13 minutes; the delta does it in 6 seconds.

For a 1 TB-class model in the Fireworks framing, their own measured numbers show 20.3 GiB deltas vs the 1024 GiB full snapshot, a ~50× reduction. PULSE's tighter, sparse encoding would push that further (extrapolating ~15 GB per delta, closer to ~65×). Either way, you are in a regime where shipping weights through commodity object storage stops being a hack and starts being the only sensible architecture.

We are not pretending this is finished. Here is the honest list.

Same scanned PDF, four outcomes: decoder availability is a deployment variable

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether a scanned PDF page can be decoded is a property of the deployment, not of the file.
  • Both samples are single pages split out of public-domain scans.
  • The English page comes from the Internet Archive's copy of the 1921 edition of Psycho-Analysis and the War Neuroses (Ferenczi, Abraham, Simmel, Jones, preface by Freud), Public Domain Mark 1.0.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether a scanned PDF page can be decoded is a property of the deployment, not of the file. In this run, the same two pages went through a handful of common PDF tools on one Apple-silicon Mac, and the outcomes were: decoded cleanly, raised an error, printed a warning and returned an empty image, and quietly listed one image layer fewer. Nothing about the PDF changed between those runs. Only the decoder that happened to be present did. Treat "could not decode" as a result your code reports, not as a gap it papers over.

Both samples are single pages split out of public-domain scans. Their page images are not plain JPEGs. The English page is stored as separate layers: a JPEG 2000 background, a JPEG 2000 foreground colour layer, and a 1-bit JBIG2 mask that carries the glyph shapes. The Chinese page uses the same kinds of encodings, two JPEG 2000 images plus a JBIG2 mask. On both, on top sits an invisible text layer added by the archive's OCR. Without that text layer, a tool that cannot read those image formats has nothing to fall back on. With it, the failure can hide.

The English page comes from the Internet Archive's copy of the 1921 edition of Psycho-Analysis and the War Neuroses (Ferenczi, Abraham, Simmel, Jones, preface by Freud), Public Domain Mark 1.0. Its reference text was proofread by hand against the page image. The Chinese page is half a page of the 1986 edition of the Simplified Character Table from the National Language Commission, also an Internet Archive item under Public Domain Mark 1.0. Two pages say little about scans in general; they only show what these two files did.

The last row is the one that deserves a design review. The text layer came back intact, so a caller that only looked at the return value would see a successful extraction. The warning was the only sign that the image half had failed. The pypdf row is quieter still, since there is not even a warning.

pdf.js loads its image decoders as wasm modules from a path the host application configures, and the last row was produced by leaving that path out; it does not mean pdf.js cannot decode these files by default. What follows is inference, not something that was run: a bundler that drops the folder, a CSP that blocks the fetch, or a serverless package that omits the files could each produce the same row without touching the PDF, and a Pillow build without OpenJPEG would behave differently from the one used here. Whoever tests locally with a full toolchain will see the clean rows and may conclude the format is handled.

A related trap sits one level down. On the English page the three layers do not hold equal amounts of text. Recognizing only the 755 by 1163 background layer returned 186 characters at a 93.62% character error rate, because that layer is the page with the writing wiped out. Recognizing the rendered whole page gave 0.26%. Decoding "an image" is not the same as decoding the right image. This is one page's layout; the Chinese page is stored differently and its first image does carry text.

In a recent development, the cheap fix is to make "decoded or not" an explicit field per image: decoded, failed with a reason, or not listed. A pipeline can then refuse to treat a text-layer-only result as complete, or route the page to a path that renders it into a plain bitmap first. OCRmyPDF is a useful contrast. By default it exits with code 6 or 2 when it meets an existing text layer; with --skip-text it writes a single log line saying the page was skipped, and exits 0 with the old layer untouched. Both can be found by a pipeline that looks, which is less true of the quieter rows above.

In a recent development, this is two pages, one machine, one run each, and the tool versions are whatever was current at the time. The Windows side and other PDF engines were not tested. Which tools lose which layer will change with versions and builds, so the table is a list of failure shapes to look for, not a ranking. The text layers on these pages also differed in quality (0.15% errors on one, 8.98% on the other), so a layer being present says nothing about it being good.

Recent findings suggest that imgIng, at https://imging.ai/ , runs PDF content extraction in the browser, merging native text with text recognized inside images. For scans whose page images are JPEG 2000 or JBIG2 encoded, it presently cannot recognize them, so such files need to be rendered to ordinary images first. That is the same rule as above, seen from the user's side.

It has been revealed that this is the kind of failure that keeps me up at night, because the worst row in your table isn't the one that errors — it's the one that looks fine. pdf.js returning empty image objects while the text layer stays intact is a silent-corruption trap: a caller checking "did I get text?" would happily ship a page with no visible content at all. Same for pypdf listing two layers instead of three with no message — the absence itself is the bug, and nothing in the output says so.

Recent findings suggest that your fix direction feels right: "decoded or not" has to be an explicit per-image field, not something inferred from whether the pipeline crashed. I'd go one step further and make a known-bad canary PDF part of the deploy itself — run it on every latest environment and fail loudly if the JBIG2 mask or JPEG 2000 layers come back empty, before any real user file touches it. A warning buried in two log lines is not a signal anyone will see in production.

One thing I'm curious about: of the four outcomes, which one would you actually design for first — the loud error, or the silent partial success? And have you thought about what a minimal canary file would need to contain to catch all three failure modes in one run?

What caught my attention wasn't just the unusually high usage consumption, but the nature of the workload.

Sources indicate that I used Sonnet 5.5 exclusively to generate relatively short PRD documents. No coding, no complex development tasks, yet the entire five-hour session allowance was exhausted in approximately 30 minutes.

Is Claude Code's usage accounting including internal processing, context operations, or background activity in a way that isn't adequately reflected in the user's visible workload?

If users cannot understand why a relatively lightweight task consumes an entire session allowance, it becomes difficult to blueprint their usage reliably.

Has Anthropic identified what is causing this behaviour, and are affected owners being investigated?

The Common Vitamin Linked To Less Belly Fat

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (473 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
  • People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
  • People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

This deeper layer of belly fat, known as visceral fat, surrounds organs such as the liver and intestines.

It matters because people with more visceral fat tend to have greater difficulty using insulin to control their blood sugar.

The link with vitamin D became weaker when the researchers took body mass index into account, suggesting that overall body size could explain part of the difference.

One possibility is that vitamin D is spread through a larger volume of tissue in people with more body fat, leaving a lower concentration in the blood.

The researchers reviewed records from nearly 1,300 adults with type 2 diabetes who attended a hospital in Quzhou, China, during a two-and-a-half-year period.

Each person had a blood test for vitamin D and a measurement to estimate their visceral fat.

The researchers divided patients into four groups according to their vitamin D levels and compared the estimated area of visceral fat in each group.

The clearest difference was between the groups with the highest and lowest vitamin D levels, with the middle groups showing a less consistent pattern.

After accounting for BMI and other differences between patients, the researchers estimated that the group with the highest vitamin D levels had about 10 square centimetres less visceral fat area than the group with the lowest levels.

Earlier research using genetic data suggested that a higher BMI can contribute to lower vitamin D levels, with weaker evidence for an effect in the other direction (Vimaleswaran et al., 2013).

As well as being distributed through a larger volume of tissue, some vitamin D may be stored in fat tissue, which could affect how much circulates in the blood.

Everyday habits could also help explain why the two measures vary together.

Someone who exercises outdoors may get more sunlight and carry less belly fat, two differences that could help explain the link.

The hospital records did not capture how much sunlight participants got, how active they were or whether they took vitamin D supplements.

Since vitamin D and belly fat were assessed at the same visit, it remains unclear which changed first or whether both were influenced by other factors.

The study was published in the Journal of International Medical Research (Zhu et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

📖 Baca

Tech Report: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.
  • Recent findings suggest that now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference.
  • Industry observers note that parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Recent findings suggest that now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

Industry observers note that parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Industry observers note that figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:.

Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create fresh variations for a target document type or language.

Sources indicate that figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry.

We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

According to recent reports, we then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

It has been revealed that A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

Sources indicate that the matched comparison indicates the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

Recent findings suggest that naViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

It has been revealed that fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it:.

Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts.

Recent findings suggest that double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output.

Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass.

Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests.

In a recent development, in the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements.

We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers.

It has been revealed that the worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth.

According to recent reports, figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label.

RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR.

Figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol.

According to recent reports, to adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output.

We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models.

We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review.

Tech Report: Eventbrite Fees vs Selling Tickets on Your Own WooCommerce Shop

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most comparisons between a hosted ticketing platform and running tickets yourself stop at a percentage.
  • I built Tickets & Passes for WooCommerce, so I have an interest here.
  • On 27 November 2026, Eventbrite's own pricing page listed a service fee of 3.7% + $1.79 per paid ticket, plus a 2.9% payment processing fee per order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most comparisons between a hosted ticketing platform and running tickets yourself stop at a percentage. The number that decides it is not only the fee. It is who pays that fee, and what you stop getting when you leave the platform.

I built Tickets & Passes for WooCommerce, so I have an interest here. I will still put the real numbers on the table first, including the parts that do not favour my plugin.

On 27 November 2026, Eventbrite's own pricing page listed a service fee of 3.7% + $1.79 per paid ticket, plus a 2.9% payment processing fee per order. Free events were listed with no platform fee. Those figures are in US dollars on the US site, and vary by country, currency and event type, so read the page for your own market. The same page states the service fee is paid by buyers by default, and that an organiser can choose to absorb it instead.

Industry observers note that A fee you pass on does not disappear. It becomes a higher price at checkout, which you pay for in conversion instead of margin.

The fixed $1.79 is what hurts cheap tickets. A $25 ticket pays a much larger share than a $50 one, which is why small venues notice the fee first.

On your own WooCommerce shop you still pay a payment provider for card processing. I am not quoting a rate, because it depends on your provider, country and volume. The fair reading is that the 2.9% line is roughly what accepting cards costs wherever you sell, and the 3.7% + $1.79 service fee is the part that stops existing when tickets run through your own shop.

That is the whole financial case, and it is enough on its own for a venue selling a few thousand tickets a year.

The plugin adds three product types to WooCommerce: Ticket for plain admission with a validity window and a number of uses, Timeslot Ticket for dated sessions with a capacity per slot, and Pass for season passes and memberships across a period. All three can sit in the same cart and order as your other products.

Recent findings suggest that every purchase complications a QR code. Staff scan it at /check-in/ on your own domain, in a phone browser, with no app to install. Each scan is decided on your server, so a cancelled ticket cannot be waved through by putting the phone in airplane mode. The readme is clear about the trade: the scanner also needs a connection at the door.

According to recent reports, around that comes what a managed platform normally supplies: a Scanner role limited to check-in, a dashboard per product type with search, manual check-in, resend, reset and cancel, and analytics charting check-ins by day and hour with CSV export. Customers find tickets in WooCommerce My Account, with an on-screen QR code, a printable PDF and an add-to-calendar file on timeslot tickets. Codes, PDFs and pass photos are served through a signed link, not a guessable URL.

The WordPress.org readme has the full steps. In outline:.

I would keep the platform in three situations. When discovery through its marketplace is where your audience actually comes from, since a saved service fee is no use against an empty room. When you have no WordPress site and no intention of running one. And for a large multi-day event with a box office team, where a managed invoice and someone else on the phone may be worth the per-ticket cost. That last one is a judgement about operations, not arithmetic.

In a recent development, run a real test purchase before launch: product page, cart, checkout, confirmation email, then a scan at the door. Check your time zone and date format. If a code will not scan, the scanner menu accepts a typed one.

To back out, deactivate the plugin. The readme claims deactivation stops it and clears its scheduled tasks while settings and records stay put, and reactivating picks up where you left off. Deleting it removes settings, scheduled tasks and the Scanner role but keeps tickets and check-in records, so removing it to test a conflict does not wipe a season of history. If you want everything gone, the TPFW_REMOVE_ALL_DATA constant in wp-config.php drops tables, QR codes, PDFs and pass photos. It cannot be undone, so take a backup and leave it out of a trial.

Work out your mix of ticket prices, apply 3.7% + $1.79 to each paid ticket, and see what a year of it totals. If that number is small next to the value of the platform's discovery and support, stay where you are. If it is not, and your venue already runs WooCommerce, this is a free way to test the operational side, with no per-ticket fee to renegotiate later.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1830 w)

Shopify Product Variants API 2026: Add Options, Create, Patch & Delete Variants in Your App

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, shopify product variants API tutorial (2026): build a real variants editor inside your Shopify app with the GraphQL Admin API - add options like Size and Colour, create every variant, edit prices and SKUs in bulk and delete variants on a real development store.
  • 💻 Free source code for this episode: https://github.com/fayyaz315/shopify-app-development-2026/tree/ep03.
  • Shopify GraphQL create product with variants: add Size and Colour options with productOptionsCreate and variantStrategy CREATE - every combination appears in one call.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, shopify product variants API tutorial (2026): build a real variants editor inside your Shopify app with the GraphQL Admin API - add options like Size and Colour, create every variant, edit prices and SKUs in bulk and delete variants on a real development store. Shopify app development series, episode 3 - everything shown is real, nothing skipped.

💻 Free source code for this episode: https://github.com/fayyaz315/shopify-app-development-2026/tree/ep03.

Shopify GraphQL create product with variants: add Size and Colour options with productOptionsCreate and variantStrategy CREATE - every combination appears in one call.

▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/0FgXgU6-9L4.

Shopify product variants API: patch the price and SKU of many variants in one call with productVariantsBulkUpdate.

▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/AwQprha84gc.

Shopify productVariantsBulkCreate and productVariantsBulkDelete: add one upcoming variant to a product, then remove variants - and check userErrors.

▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/qy4VBIGcjKA.

Sources indicate that in the next ten minutes, you'll turn one product into every size and colour it comes in, from inside your own Shopify app. Set one price for every variant, and save them all in a single call, add a fresh size, delete the colour you don't sell, and see every call in GraphiQL first, with Shopify's real responses. This is the Shopify product variants API, running inside our own Shopify app.

Sources indicate that right now this hoodie has exactly one variant. This is episode three of the Shopify app development series. Episode two built the products page; today every product gets sizes and colours.

The full code is free on GitHub, and the link is in the description.

First, the two words that confuse everyone: options and variants. An option is a choice the customer makes, like size or colour. Each option has values: small, medium, large.

In a recent development, black and grey. And a variant is one combination you actually sell. Three sizes times two colours is six variants, and each one has its own price, SKU and stock.

Every product has at least one variant. A product with no options still has one, called Default Title. That's the one you saw a second ago.

So the rule for the whole video: options describe the choices, and variants are the rows you sell. Why does this matter for an app? Because the price, the SKU and the stock all live on the variant, never on the product.

Sources indicate that now our app. Every request takes the same path as in episode two. The page asks the loader for data, and buttons call the action.

Recent findings suggest that both run on the server and talk to the Admin GraphQL API, version 2026-10. No upcoming permission is needed. The write products scope from episode two already covers options and variants.

Sources indicate that on the products page, I search for hoodie. There's our Classic Zip Hoodie, and a latest column highlights how many variants it has. The product title is now a link to the new page.

Sources indicate that one line in the products route. I click it, and the product page opens inside the admin. The new route file is app.products_.$id.

Recent findings suggest that the $id is the product number in the URL. And the underscore matters: without it, this page would nest inside the products page layout. With it, it's a page of its own.

In a recent development, let's read the product first, and as always, I test every call in GraphiQL before it goes into the app. One product by ID, with its options, and up to ten variants with ID, title, price and SKU. There's the proof: one option called Title, one value Default Title, and one variant at $0.

In a recent development, and notice the cost at the bottom: a small query like this costs only a few points out of two thousand. In the app, the query lives at the top of the fresh route. Options give me the name and values for the badges.

Recent findings suggest that and variants give one row each: title, price, SKU and inventory. The loader turns the number from the URL back into a global ID, runs the query, and returns a not found response if the product doesn't exist.

Industry observers note that now let's add options. This is how you create a product with variants through the GraphQL API. The option is Size, and the values are S, M and L, separated by commas.

Add, and the toast indicates Size added, three variants. Default Title is gone. Then a second option: Color, with black and grey.

It has been revealed that six variants. Every size in every colour, created in one call. Each newly introduced row starts at $0 and no SKU.

Recent findings suggest that that's why the next step is a bulk edit. Here's that call in GraphiQL. productOptionsCreate, with the product ID, the options, and variantStrategy CREATE.

Recent findings suggest that the response demonstrates the option with its three values, and three variants: S, M and L, each at $0. Look at the first ID. It's the old Default Title variant, renamed to S.

It has been revealed that shopify reuses it instead of deleting it. In the app, this is the whole mutation. The key word is CREATE.

According to recent reports, it tells Shopify to make a variant for every upcoming combination. Leave it out, and the default is leave as is: the values are added, but no new variants are made. That surprises a lot of people.

The action splits the comma list into values, sends one option, and puts the new variant count in the toast. Every branch ends with this little done helper. If Shopify sends userErrors, the page shows them.

If not, it shows the success message.

Now prices. Six variants at $0 is not a shop. I type forty nine into price for all variants and click apply to all.

In a recent development, every row now says forty nine, and I give the first two variants a SKU. Nothing is saved yet: it's only on the page. Then save variants.

It has been revealed that one click, one API call, six variants saved. In GraphiQL it's productVariantsBulkUpdate: the product ID, and a list of variants, each with its ID, a price and a SKU. The response gives back every variant with its newly introduced price and SKU.

Three variants, one request. And the same call works for one variant or a hundred, so you never loop over single updates. Here's the mutation in the app.

It has been revealed that watch the SKU. It isn't a field on the variant input anymore. It goes inside inventory item.

The action maps every row into that shape: ID, price, and inventory item with the SKU. On the page, apply to all only changes local state. Nothing hits Shopify until you press save, so one save is one call.

Next, a size we forgot: XL. Add variant opens a form with one field per option. Size XL, colour black, price fifty four, and a SKU.

Added. Seven variants, and look at the Size option: XL is there now, and I never created it. That's the Shopify GraphQL way: you send option names and values, and Shopify keeps the option list in sync.

In a recent development, in GraphiQL, productVariantsBulkCreate takes a list of variants. Each one names its optionValues: option name Size, value XL. The newly introduced variant comes back with its ID, the price twenty nine, and the SKU.

In a recent development, in the app, the mutation is the same shape as the revision. The action sends one variant: its optionValues, a price, and the SKU inside inventory item. On the page, the form builds those optionValues from the product's own options, so it works for any product.

Industry observers note that and if you send a combination that already exists, Shopify refuses with a user error that the variant already exists. My done helper indicates it as an error toast.

Now delete. We don't sell grey after all, so I tick the three grey variants. Delete selected asks first, because this can't be undone.

Three deleted. And grey has disappeared from the Color option too: a value with no variants is removed. In GraphiQL, productVariantsBulkDelete takes the product ID and a list of variant IDs.

In a recent development, XL is gone, and the variant count is back to three, with no userErrors. In the app, that's this mutation. The page keeps the ticked IDs in state, and the action sends all of them in one call.

Last, the whole Color option. Only black is left, so it doesn't add anything. I click the bin next to Color.

Option deleted, and the variants are simply S, M, L and XL. That's productOptionsDelete with the product ID and the option ID. One catch, tested on my store: with two colours still in use, Shopify refuses.

The error states cannot delete an option with multiple values.

Recent findings suggest that now the page itself, built with Polaris web components. Each row has a checkbox for delete, then the price and SKU as real input fields, right inside the table. An honest bug I hit while recording: after adding Size, the option form still held Size, so my second option became Size Color.

Industry observers note that the fix: after every successful save, I bump a form key, and React remounts both forms empty. Then I recorded again. The same effect shows the toast and closes whichever modal is open.

A few honest notes before the recap. One: my query loads the first hundred variants. That's plenty for most products, but a major catalog needs pagination, like the products page in episode two.

In a recent development, two: inventory still claims zero. Stock lives on locations, and that's its own episode. Three: every one of these mutations can succeed over HTTP and still refuse your input.

Recent findings suggest that always read userErrors. And a bonus: everything you saw was tested on my real development store before I pressed record.

Recent findings suggest that so, the recap. Read options and variants with one product query. Add options with productOptionsCreate and the CREATE strategy.

Change prices and SKUs in bulk, add single variants with bulk create, and delete with bulk delete. Want to practise? Add a compare at price column, or a button that copies one variant's SKU pattern to every row.

That's the Shopify product variants API, working inside a real app, on a real store. The full code for this episode is free on GitHub. The link is in the description.

Next episode: collections. Manual ones, smart ones with rules, and adding products to them. See you there.

#149329. Industry News: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

📅 24 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (667 w)

Industry News: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

📅 24 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense.
  • In a recent development, in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R.
  • The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. Fresh research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.

In a recent development, in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.

The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.

How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together.

Different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.

"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh indicates.

According to recent reports, the researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.

Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree.

It has been revealed that to explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.

According to recent reports, during the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.

Recent findings suggest that the results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions promptly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.

"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.

A Possible Brainwide Consensus Mechanism.

The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.

"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.

If dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.

According to recent reports, the idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.

"While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole.".

#149325. Tech Report: Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain

📅 28 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (942 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that coffee may affect far more than alertness.
  • Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.
  • The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that coffee may affect far more than alertness. Latest research suggests that both regular and decaffeinated coffee can alter the gut microbiome and may influence mood, stress, memory, and attention through the gut brain connection.

Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.

The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.

How Coffee May Affect the Gut-Brain Connection.

Scientists have long studied coffee for possible effects on digestion, mood, and overall health, but exactly how these effects arise has remained less clear.

Industry observers note that the new research focused on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking microorganisms in the digestive tract with the brain. Signals can travel between the gut and brain through immune activity, hormones, nerves, and chemical compounds produced by microbes.

According to recent reports, researchers examined 31 regular coffee drinkers and 31 people who did not normally drink coffee. Participants completed psychological assessments and kept records of caffeine intake and diet. Researchers also collected stool and urine samples to track changes in gut microbes, metabolism, mood, and perceived stress.

For the study, 'Coffee drinkers' were set as those who regularly consume 3-5 cups of coffee a day, defined by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) as a safe and moderate amount for most people.

What Happened When Coffee Was Removed.

According to recent reports, the regular coffee drinkers first stopped consuming coffee for two weeks. During that period, participants repeatedly completed psychological assessments and provided stool and urine samples.

According to recent reports, when coffee drinkers stopped drinking coffee, researchers observed substantial shifts in their gut metabolite profiles compared with people who did not normally consume coffee. Metabolites are small molecules produced or altered during metabolism, including compounds created by gut microbes as they process food and other substances.

Coffee was then reintroduced without participants knowing whether they were receiving caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee. Half received decaf, while the other half received caffeinated coffee.

In a recent development, after coffee returned to their diets, both groups reported lower perceived stress, depression and impulsivity scores. The findings suggest that some of coffee's effects on mood may not depend entirely on caffeine.

Coffee Was Linked to Changes in Gut Bacteria.

Researchers also found differences in several types of gut bacteria.

Bacteria, such as 'Eggertella sp.' or 'Cryptobacterium curtum', were more abundant among coffee drinkers than non-coffee drinkers. 'Eggertella sp' is thought to contribute to acid secretion in the stomach and intestines, while 'Cryptobacterium curtum' may participate in bile acid production.

Both processes could potentially help create an intestinal environment that discourages certain harmful bacteria and infections.

Researchers also observed higher levels of 'Firmicutes' bacteria, a broad group of microbes that has previously been associated with positive emotions in females.

Decaf and Caffeinated Coffee Showed Different Effects.

One of the most intriguing findings was that caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee did not appear to affect participants in exactly the same way.

Improved learning and memory were observed only among participants drinking decaffeinated coffee. That finding suggests that substances other than caffeine may contribute to some of coffee's effects on cognition.

Coffee contains thousands of chemical compounds, including polyphenols. These plant derived substances can act as antioxidants and can also interact with gut microbes, potentially influencing metabolism and other biological processes.

Sources indicate that caffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was associated with reduced feelings of anxiety as well as improved vigilance and attention. Caffeine was also linked to a reduced risk of inflammation.

Recent findings suggest that because the study involved a relatively small number of participants, the findings do not establish that coffee directly causes these changes in mood, cognition, or gut health. However, they provide new clues about the biological pathways that could help explain associations reported in earlier coffee research.

Sources indicate that corresponding author of the study, Professor John Cryan, Principal Investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork, commented: "Public interest in gut health has risen hugely. The relationship between digestive and mental health is also increasingly being better understood, but the mechanisms behind coffee's effects on this gut-brain axis have remained unclear.

"Our findings reveal the microbiome and neurological responses to coffee, as well as their potential long-term benefits for a healthier microbiome. Coffee may modify what microbes do collectively, and what metabolites they use. As the public continues to think about dietary changes for the right digestive balance, coffee has the potential to also be harnessed as a further intervention as part of a healthy balanced diet.".

The findings add to growing evidence that coffee should not be viewed simply as a source of caffeine. Its many other components may interact with the microbiome, metabolism, and nervous system in different ways.

"Coffee is more than just caffeine -- it's a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism, and even our emotional well-being," said Professor Cryan. "Our findings suggest that coffee, whether caffeinated or decaffeinated, can influence health in distinct but complementary ways.".

Materials provided by University College Cork. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#149322. Industry News: Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (894 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone.
  • In a recent development, fresh research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces.
  • Industry observers note that researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone. The faces that capture a child's attention could provide crucial clues about their mental health and how depression develops.

In a recent development, fresh research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces. The pattern appears to differ depending on whether a child has a family history of depression.

Industry observers note that researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time. By identifying these patterns while children are still developing, scientists hope to better understand who may be at greater risk and eventually improve prevention strategies.

"Most of the vulnerabilities that we focus on are still developing during this time period," remarked Brandon Gibb, director of the Mood Disorders Institute and SUNY distinguished professor of psychology. "You can catch things as they're developing, rather than only studying them once they're already there and pretty stable.".

Following Children's Attention Over Time.

Earlier research has linked depression with greater attention to sad faces. However, those associations have generally been modest, and scientists have not been sure whether biased attention contributes to depression or develops because of it.

The Binghamton study was designed to investigate that question by tracking both depressive symptoms and attention patterns over time. According to the researchers, it is the first study to examine how changes in each may predict later changes in the other among children.

"The real novel piece is that we looked at these transactional relations," remarked Kelly Gair, a PhD student at Binghamton and lead author of the paper. "Between attentional biases and depressive symptoms, we looked at the way that they were mutually predicting one another across the time points, which is especially novel and hasn't been done before.".

The research team, which also included Leslie A. Brick from the University of Latest Mexico, followed 242 children and their mothers for two years. Participants were assessed every six months.

During each visit, children viewed pairs of faces on a screen. One face showed a neutral expression, while the other displayed an emotion (happy, sad, or angry). Eye tracking technology measured which face held the child's attention and for how long.

Recent findings suggest that children in the study looked at faces conveying different emotions onscreen, and eye tracking technology recorded where their attention veered. Photo credit: NimStim Set of Facial Expressions (Tottenham et al., 2009).

Family History Changes the Pattern.

The results suggest that increasing depressive symptoms do not affect every child's attention in the same way. Family history appeared to play an important role.

Among children whose mothers had a history of major depressive disorder, rising depressive symptoms were associated with greater attention to sad faces. In other words, as these children experienced more symptoms themselves, their attention became increasingly drawn toward expressions of sadness.

"For those who are already at risk, the more these children experience depression themselves, the more they lose their ability to pull their attention away from the sad things around them," Gibb mentioned.

"We know that when you're depressed, it changes what you pay attention to," Gair said. "Our results suggest that these changes may be more long-lasting and may differ depending on family history. One thought is that for children of mothers with depression, who are exposed to more facial displays of sadness from interactions with their mom, these types of facial expressions become even more salient when they experience depression themselves, so their attention becomes increasingly stuck on sad expressions.".

Happy Faces May Lose Their Pull.

A different pattern emerged among children whose mothers had no history of depression.

When depressive symptoms increased in these children, they did not become more focused on sad expressions. Instead, they paid less attention to happy faces.

"In our lower-risk children, what seems to be happening is that experiences of depression are eroding a protective factor, which is how much they pay attention to happy faces," Gibb said.

According to recent reports, the distinction suggests that depression may alter emotional attention through different pathways depending on a child's underlying level of familial risk. For some children, sadness may become increasingly difficult to ignore. For others, positive emotional signals may simply become less likely to capture their attention.

Industry observers note that the researchers are continuing to follow the children as they enter adolescence, a period when the risk of developing depression increases for many young people. They hope to determine whether these early attention patterns are associated with a greater likelihood of receiving a depression diagnosis later on.

The paper, "Transactional Relations Between Attentional Biases for Affective Stimuli and Depressive Symptoms in Offspring of Mothers With and Without Major Depressive Disorder," was published in the Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science.

Materials provided by Binghamton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.
  • Lowering sugar consumption by about one can of soda and adding one half-cup of fibre-rich foods daily reduces abdominal fat and type 2 diabetes risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Lowering sugar consumption by about one can of soda and adding one half-cup of fibre-rich foods daily reduces abdominal fat and type 2 diabetes risk.

A study has found that decreasing about 47 grams of sugar intake per day — equivalent to a can of soda — lowers insulin secretion, on average, by 33 percent.

Increasing fibre intake by 5 grams a day — the amount in a half cup of beans — results in a 10 percent reduction of belly fat.

Visceral fat is a type of body fat stored within the abdominal area and internal organs.

This type of fat causes abdominal obesity and is also associated with several health problems, like type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer.

Dr Emily Ventura and colleagues conducted a 16-week study on overweight Latino adolescents who were between 12 to 19 years old.

They tested if increasing fiber consumption and decreasing sugar intake have an effect on type 2 diabetes risk factors.

“A reduction in visceral fat indicates a reduction in risk for type 2 diabetes, considering that to a greater degree than total body fat, visceral fat [fat surrounding the internal organs] has been shown to be negatively associated with insulin sensitivity.”.

Industry observers note that those who increased fiber intake had a significant reduction in body mass index (-2 percent vs. 2 percent) and visceral adipose tissue (-10 percent vs. no change) compared with those who decreased fiber intake.”.

Being overweight or obese are serious problems affecting adults and children around the world.

The World Health Organization reports that in 2016 over 1.9 billion adults were overweight and more than 650 million adults were obese.

The authors of this study wrote:.

“Our results suggest that intensive interventions may not be necessary to achieve modifications in sugar and fiber intake.

Accordingly, nutritional guidance given in the primary care or community setting may be sufficient to promote the suggested dietary changes in some individuals.

In addition, policies that promote reduced intake of added sugar and increased intake of fiber could be effective public health strategies for the prevention of type 2 diabetes in this high-risk population.”.

The study was published in the Archives of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine (Ventura et al., 2009).

#149317. Latest Update: Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging
